Because the service does not verify authorization before retrieving credentials from the shared store, it injects the target tenant's application programming interface (API) keys into the request. This flaw allows an attacker to perform unauthorized requests and consume another tenant's large language model (LLM) resources and quotas.

items.title: identrail: Cross-tenant GitHub installation binding without ownership verification
items.summary: identrail is a machine identity security platform for AWS, GitHub/OIDC, and Kubernetes. Prior to 1.0.2, the default-on `POST /v1/workspaces/:workspace_id/projects/:project_id/github/connect/complete` endpoint in `internal/api/router.go` accepts `installation_id` from the request body or `X-GitHub-Installation-ID` header without verifying the installation belongs to the caller's workspace. `CompleteGitHubConnection` in `internal/api/github_connect.go` rigorously binds `state` to the caller's tenant, workspace, and project, but checks only that the installation ID is positive before persisting it as the caller's connection. `ListInstallationRepositories` in `internal/connectors/github/repositories.go` invokes token creation through `internal/connectors/github/app.go` and `POST /app/installations/{installationId}/access_tokens`, using the application's JWT. An authenticated tenant who starts a legitimate connection can supply another customer's non-secret installation ID to read the victim organization's private repository inventory, content, and metadata or drive posture scans, provided identrail's GitHub App is installed there. The default-off V2 `CompleteGitHubConnector` path shares the installation-ownership gap and additionally matches pending `state` without rechecking caller scope. This issue is fixed in version 1.0.2.

items.title: OpenHop: Path Traversal in Flow ID File Operations
items.summary: OpenHop is a tool for creating interactive data-flow diagrams. Prior to 0.3.7, `@openhop/server` passes unauthenticated flow route parameters from `GET /api/flows/:id` and `DELETE /api/flows/:id` in `packages/server/src/routes.ts` to `FlowStore.filePath()` in `packages/server/src/store.ts` without an identifier allow-list. The router applies `decodeURIComponent` to the id, and `path.join()` then normalizes traversal outside the configured flow directory after appending the .yaml extension. An attacker can read accessible YAML files as YAML-parsed JSON or permanently delete accessible .yaml files outside that directory, exposing configuration or secrets and disrupting dependent services. In `packages/server/src/index.ts`, CORS `origin: true` permits any browser origin, enabling a malicious webpage to target a loopback-bound instance. Docker deployments default to `HOST=0.0.0.0` and permit direct unauthenticated network access. This issue is fixed in repository release 0.3.7.

items.title: vLLM: Permissive default CORS origins allow cross-origin requests to the vLLM HTTP server
items.summary:
### Summary

The OpenAI-compatible server registers Starlette `CORSMiddleware` with
`allowed_origins` defaulting to `["*"]`, and performs no authentication unless
`--api-key` (or `VLLM_API_KEY`) is configured. A web page on any origin can send
requests to a vLLM server that the victim's browser can reach (for example
`localhost` or an internal/VPN address) and read the responses. The default
`allow_credentials=False` blocks cookie-bearing cross-origin requests; because
vLLM authenticates with a bearer header rather than cookies, the wildcard still
permits untokenized access to an unauthenticated server and read access when the
caller already holds a token.

### Details

Affected components

- `vllm/entrypoints/launchers/cli_args.py` - `allowed_origins` default value.
- `vllm/entrypoints/serve/middleware/register.py` - `CORSMiddleware`
  registration.
- `vllm/entrypoints/serve/middleware/authenticate.py` - auth middleware and its
  guarded path prefixes.

 Root cause

`vllm/entrypoints/launchers/cli_args.py`:

```python
allow_credentials: bool = False
"""Allow credentials."""
allowed_origins: list[str] = field(default_factory=lambda: ["*"])
"""Allowed origins."""
```

`vllm/entrypoints/serve/middleware/register.py`:

```python
app.add_middleware(
    CORSMiddleware,
    allow_origins=args.allowed_origins,
    allow_credentials=args.allow_credentials,
    allow_methods=args.allowed_methods,
    allow_headers=args.allowed_headers,
)
```

The auth middleware is added only when a token is configured and guards only the
`/v1`, `/v2`, `/inference`, and `/cohere` prefixes. `/v1/load_lora_adapter` and
`/v1/unload_lora_adapter` are inside `/v1` and therefore do require a key when
one is set; they are open only when no key is configured and dynamic LoRA
updating is enabled.

### Impact


- A malicious page can enumerate models (`GET /v1/models`), issue
  `POST /v1/chat/completions`, consume GPU time, and read model output through
  the victim's browser.
- When the server is reachable only from the victim's network, the browser acts
  as a proxy a remote website could not otherwise use.
- With `allow_credentials=False`, cookie-based CSRF does not apply; the exposure
  is cross-origin request execution and response disclosure.

This advisory was fixed in [MR61009](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/61009).

items.title: YosemiteCrew: Missing organization authorization on service and PMS library/template routes
items.summary: YosemiteCrew provides organization-based service and task management. In the source-reported affected main and dev snapshots, YosemiteCrew's service and PMS task-library/template routes omit organization and permission checks. `authorizeCognito` in `apps/backend/src/middlewares/auth.ts` sets the authenticated user's ID but does not provide the `withOrgPermissions()` and `requirePermission(...)` checks used by protected siblings. In `apps/backend/src/routers/service.router.ts`, `PATCH /fhir/v1/service/:id` and `DELETE /fhir/v1/service/:id` are authentication-only, while `GET /fhir/v1/service/:id` has no authentication middleware. The trace through `apps/backend/src/controllers/web/service.controller.ts` to `apps/backend/src/services/service.service.ts` passes a global record ID into `ServiceModel.findById(oid)` without an `organisationId` filter. In `apps/backend/src/routers/task.router.ts`, `PUT /v1/task/pms/library/:libraryId`, `POST /v1/task/pms/templates`, `PATCH /v1/task/pms/templates/:templateId` and `DELETE /v1/task/pms/templates/:templateId` likewise lack organization/role enforcement. Any registered platform user, including a patient/companion-app account, can modify or delete another organization's service catalogue and PMS task-library/template data, affecting bookings and billing; service records can additionally be read without authentication. An earlier security change protected create routes but left these sibling operations exposed. A fixed release cannot be established from the available evidence.

items.title: Waline login accepts a non-string email as a match-all MongoDB query
items.summary: Waline is a comment system with backend support. Prior to version 1.41.1, the login endpoint POST /api/token reads the email field from the request body without checking its type and passes it straight into the MongoDB storage query. When email is not a string (for example a JSON object such as {"$ne": null}), the MongoDB storage adapter's parseWhere silently DROPS the field rather than rejecting the request, producing an empty filter that matches ALL users. The endpoint then verifies the submitted password against the FIRST user returned (user[0]), which in Waline is the first-registered user — the site administrator. This is a PARTIAL authentication bypass, not a full one. The attacker still needs a valid password for that first user; this is not a zero-knowledge bypass and it does not disclose passwords. Its concrete effects are: (1) the email/identifier factor is removed for the administrator account, (2) user enumeration (a non-string email never fails the "no such user" branch), and (3) credential-stuffing amplification — an attacker can test a leaked or weak password against the administrator account without knowing the administrator's email. This issue has been patched in version 1.41.1.

items.title: calipso: keep BIG TCP payload_len in calipso_skbuff_setattr()
items.summary:
In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

calipso: keep BIG TCP payload_len in calipso_skbuff_setattr()

calipso_skbuff_setattr() adjusts payload_len by the length of the
option it inserts or resizes:

	payload = ntohs(ip6_hdr->payload_len);
	ip6_hdr->payload_len = htons(payload + len_delta);

GRO can build BIG TCP packets larger than IPV6_MAXPLEN, and stores
payload_len == 0 for them; ipv6_payload_len() then falls back to
skb->len.  For such a packet forwarded to a destination mapped to
CALIPSO, the code above writes len_delta (or 65536 + len_delta when
shrinking) into payload_len, and ipv6_payload_len() no longer falls
back to skb->len.  nf_tables, conntrack and sch_cake rely on it.

The same arithmetic also wraps when a packet grows past IPV6_MAXPLEN,
and a BIG TCP packet that shrinks below IPV6_MAXPLEN should get its
real length back.

Set payload_len from the skb length with ipv6_set_payload_len(), which
stores 0 above IPV6_MAXPLEN and the real length otherwise, as
ipv6_gro_complete() does.  The network header was just reset to
skb->data, so skb->len - sizeof(*ip6_hdr) is the payload length.

Tested on one kernel (arm64, QEMU) with SELinux permissive, a minimal
mdp-generated policy (network_peer_controls=1), "netlabelctl calipso
add pass doi:16" and a NetLabel mapping of fd00:2::/64 to CALIPSO
DOI 16.  calipso_skbuff_setattr() was called through
netlbl_skbuff_setattr() from a test-only debugfs hook (not part of

path, with a client injecting unlabeled UDP through a router to a

items.title: Vue I18n: escapeParameter does not prevent XSS through srcdoc in translation messages
items.summary: Vue I18n is the internationalization plugin for Vue.js. From 11.1.10 until 11.4.14 and from 12.0.0-alpha.4 until 12.0.0-alpha.5, sanitizeTranslatedHtml() escapes markup and event-handler text inside an iframe srcdoc value but leaves the srcdoc attribute active. Browsers decode the character references and parse the value as a same-origin nested HTML document, allowing attacker-controlled parameters or translation content placed in srcdoc to execute script when applications enable escapeParameter and render translations as HTML through v-html. Versions 9.14.5 and 10.0.8 are also affected and are no longer supported, while i18n-t rendering is not affected. This issue is fixed in versions 11.4.14 and 12.0.0-alpha.5.

items.title: Unvalidated pin index in GPIO syscall handlers allows out-of-bounds kernel writes from user mode
items.summary:
The GPIO syscall handlers in drivers/gpio/gpio_handlers.c did not validate the pin argument supplied by a user-mode caller. z_vrfy_gpio_pin_configure(), z_vrfy_gpio_pin_get_config() and z_vrfy_gpio_pin_interrupt_configure() verified only the device object (K_SYSCALL_DRIVER_GPIO() / K_SYSCALL_OBJ()) and then passed the caller-supplied gpio_pin_t straight through to z_impl_gpio_pin_*() and on to the driver. The only pin check in include/zephyr/drivers/gpio.h was __ASSERT(gpio_port_pin_is_supported(cfg->port_pin_mask, pin), ...), which compiles to nothing unless CONFIG_ASSERT is enabled, so in a production build no check existed at all.

GPIO drivers use pin as a shift count and as an array index on the documented assumption that it is a pin the controller supports. On STM32, for example, gpio_stm32_pin_interrupt_configure() turns pin into an EXTI line and stm32_gpio_intc_set_irq_callback() writes data->cb[line_num].cb and data->cb[line_num].data into a NUM_EXTI_LINES-entry array (default 16) in drivers/interrupt_controller/intc_gpio_stm32.c, guarded only by a compiled-out __ASSERT_NO_MSG(); the same function then reads exti_irq_table[line_num] and calls irq_enable() on the result. Other controllers index fixed-size per-pin configuration tables the same way — drivers/gpio/gpio_ite_it8xxx2_v2.c reads an MMIO base pointer out of wuc_base[8] with the caller's pin and performs a read-modify-write through it.

The issue is reachable only in builds with CONFIG_USERSPACE=y (the file is compiled under that symbol), by a user-mode thread that has been granted access to a GPIO device object. Such a grant is intended to authorize control of that port's pins; the missing validation instead lets the thread drive a supervisor-mode out-of-bounds write of a function pointer and an associated void * past a kernel .bss array, and out-of-bounds reads that feed irq_enable() and MMIO accesses — an escape from the user-mode sandbox that can lead to kernel memory corruption, arbitrary code execution, or a crash.

The fix validates pin against the controller's gpio_driver_config.port_pin_mask with gpio_port_pin_is_supported() in every pin-taking z_vrfy_ handler and returns -EINVAL otherwise, complemented by an unconditional pin >= GPIO_MAX_PINS_PER_PORT range check added to the shared z_impl_gpio_pin_*() inlines.

items.title: NORA missing cross-user token-management authorization
items.summary: NORA is a self-hosted artifact registry and pull-through cache. Prior to 0.9.5, `nora-registry` authenticates the token-management UI but fails to require administrator authorization. `auth_middleware()` protects `/ui/tokens` and `/api/ui/tokens`, but state-changing requests are checked only with `role.can_write()`, not `role.can_admin()`. `tokens_page()` and `tokens_list()` call `store.list_all_tokens()`, exposing IDs and metadata across all users, while `tokens_revoke()` calls `store.revoke_token` using the supplied token ID without an ownership or admin check. A read bearer token can enumerate other users' token existence, owner, role, description, expiry and last-use metadata. A write bearer token or write-capable OIDC identity can additionally revoke arbitrary admin and service tokens, disrupting the registry and forcing credential recovery. Read-only identities cannot POST a revocation. This issue is fixed in version 0.9.5.

items.title: ocfs2/dlm: Protect the recovery list during debugfs reads
items.summary:
In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

ocfs2/dlm: Protect the recovery list during debugfs reads

Recovery participant records must remain alive while debug_state_print()
walks reco.node_data and formats their fields. The formatter holds
dlm->spinlock, but the recovery participant list is protected by
dlm_reco_state_lock. In particular, dlm_destroy_recovery_area() detaches
the list under dlm_reco_state_lock and frees the detached records after
releasing it. A concurrent debugfs open can therefore read freed memory.

Protect the participant traversal and field reads in debug_state_print()
with dlm_reco_state_lock, matching the existing list writers. This also
serializes the traversal against list_add_tail() during recovery-area
initialization. Make the existing lock available to the debug code
through dlmcommon.h; the lock remains internal to the OCFS2 DLM module.

Release dlm->spinlock after formatting the other domain state and before
acquiring dlm_reco_state_lock, so the debug reader does not nest the two
locks. Leave recovery list insertion, detachment and freeing unchanged.

items.title: net: stmmac: dwmac1000: clear the RGMII status interrupt
items.summary:
In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

net: stmmac: dwmac1000: clear the RGMII status interrupt

Since commit 2e2c878a3141 ("net: stmmac: remove SGMII/RGMII/SMII
interrupt handling") nothing on the RGMII path reads GMAC_RGSMIIIS, so
RGSMIIIS stays pending behind GMAC_INT_MASK from the first link change
on. stmmac_resume() resets the MAC in stmmac_hw_setup(); the reset sets
GMAC_INT_MASK to 0 until dwmac1000_core_init() writes the mask again,
and the pending status storms the line:

  dwmac_dma_interrupt: unexpected status 04000000

A register dump at the first message on ODROID-HC4 showed it:

  core int_status 00000001 int_mask 00000000 pmt 00000000 rgsmiiis 0000000d

When the resume thread runs on the CPU that takes the MAC interrupt,
the storm starves it: a soft lockup, then a watchdog reset or a hang.

Read GMAC_RGSMIIIS in dwmac1000_irq_status() when the status is not
masked, as the driver did before 2e2c878a3141; the read clears it.

Wake-on-LAN resume from s2idle with the resume thread and the MAC
interrupt on one CPU: Helios64 (dwmac-rk), 7.3-rc6, soft-locked in 3 of
3 resumes without a fix and in 0 of 10 with this patch; it ran with an
out-of-tree dwmac-rk change that keeps the GMAC powered across suspend.
ODROID-HC4 (dwmac-meson8b): 0 of 10 with this patch, 2 of 2 without a
fix on a 7.3-rc5 build. irq_rgmii_n went up by one per resume.

items.title: autofs: ignore notification errors from a replaced pipe
items.summary:
In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

autofs: ignore notification errors from a replaced pipe

autofs_notify_daemon() takes a reference to the current notification
pipe under wq_mutex, then drops the mutex before writing the request. The
write can block while the daemon enters catatonic mode and installs a
replacement pipe.

If the old pipe's reader is then closed, the delayed write returns -EPIPE
and the generic error path enters catatonic mode again. That transition
acts on the current superblock state, closes the replacement pipe, and
releases the new daemon generation's wait queues.

Only enter catatonic mode when the pipe which failed is still the current
pipe. Factor the already-locked transition so the identity check and state
change are atomic with respect to another replacement.

This was reproduced on v7.3-rc5-337-gff47652a4b66c in a local QEMU guest.
An unprivileged UID 65534 lookup filled the old packet pipe before a
normal CATATONIC/SETPIPEFD restart. On the unmodified kernel, the new pipe
received HUP and both a pending victim lookup and a later lookup failed
with ENOENT in two out of two fresh-mount runs.

With this change, the new pipe remained active, received an intact
304-byte request, and both victim lookups completed in two out of two
runs. Normal lookup and restart-without-a-blocked-writer controls passed.
No KASAN, oops, refcount, or lock diagnostic was observed. A source
reproducer and complete local logs are available privately on request.

The demonstrated impact is limited to denial of a shared autofs service
during a legitimate daemon restart. No memory corruption, information leak,
privilege escalation, or code execution primitive was observed.

items.title: KVM: nVMX: Reset MMU back to the root MMU if loading L2 state fails for !VM-Entry
items.summary:
In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

KVM: nVMX: Reset MMU back to the root MMU if loading L2 state fails for !VM-Entry

Reset the vCPU's MMU pointer back to the root MMU if loading L2 state fails
in the "not from VM-Entry" case, i.e. when emulating RSM or handling
KVM_SET_NESTED_STATE.  Failure to unwind the MMU pointer results in KVM
trying to run L1 with a nested MMU, and is especially problematic if the
vCPU manages to free its nested state before the VM crashes.  Constructing
the root for a nested EPT MMU goes through vmcs12, which is dynamically
allocated/freed when nVMX is enabled/disabled.  And so if the nested state
is freed with the MMU still pointing at the nested MMU, KVM will hit a NULL
pointer deref when attempting to get L1=>L2 EPTP.

  BUG: kernel NULL pointer dereference, address: 0000000000000078
  #PF: supervisor read access in kernel mode
  #PF: error_code(0x0000) - not-present page
  PGD 114a2d067 P4D 111743067 PUD 11141f067 PMD 0
  Oops: Oops: 0000 [#1] SMP
  CPU: 20 UID: 1000 PID: 1272 Comm: nested_tdp_faul Not tainted 7.3.0-rc4-8c89f11d1a99b-sink-vm #1914 PREEMPTLAZY
  Hardware name: QEMU Standard PC (Q35 + ICH9, 2009), BIOS 0.0.0 02/06/2015

items.title: sctp: revalidate output stream after association connect wait
items.summary:
In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

sctp: revalidate output stream after association connect wait

When message interleaving is enabled, the first send waits for association
establishment before building its data chunks.  The wait drops the socket
lock, and handshake processing can reduce the output stream count to the
peer-advertised inbound stream count.  sctp_stream_init() then frees the
extension of every removed stream.

The sender resumes with the stream that it checked before the wait.  If the
peer removed that stream, sctp_outq_tail() later dereferences its NULL
extension.  Fatal-oops policies then panic the host.

KASAN: null-ptr-deref in range [0x38-0x3f]
RIP: sctp_outq_tail+0x49e/0xaa0
Call Trace:
 sctp_primitive_SEND
 sctp_sendmsg_to_asoc
 sctp_sendmsg

A range check alone is insufficient.  Stream reconfiguration can grow the
output count again while the lock is released without recreating extensions
freed by the earlier shrink.  The stream can then be in range while its
extension remains NULL.  The send-buffer wait has the same issue.

Factor the range and extension checks into a helper and repeat both after
each send-path wait that drops the socket lock.  Once the lock is
reacquired, the validation remains stable through data creation and
queueing.

If validation fails after the connect wait, the auto-created association is
already established.  Return ESRCH so the existing caller path keeps it
under state-machine ownership instead of freeing it directly, which would
leave protocol, counter and socket state inconsistent.

items.title: scsi: libiscsi: Validate the ITT reflected in a Reject PDU
items.summary:
In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

scsi: libiscsi: Validate the ITT reflected in a Reject PDU

A Reject PDU carries a copy of the header it rejects, and
iscsi_handle_reject() takes the ITT out of that copy to find the task to
clean up:

      memcpy(&rejected_pdu, data, sizeof(struct iscsi_hdr));
      ...
      task = iscsi_itt_to_task(conn, rejected_pdu.itt);

That value is whatever the target put there. iscsi_itt_to_task() bounds
the index against cmds_max and checks nothing else, so any task in the
pool can be named, and iscsi_nop_out_rsp() then completes it.

An index that has never been used gives a NULL task->conn: the pool is
zeroed at session setup and conn is assigned only when a task is
allocated. If the task was used and returned, iscsi_complete_task() hits
its WARN_ON_ONCE(task->state == ISCSI_TASK_FREE) and the refcount
underflows. An in-flight SCSI command is completed as successful - a 1
MiB read returned 1048576 with none of its buffer written and no
warning.

Validate the reflected ITT the way iscsi_itt_to_ctask() validates a
command ITT, and require the task to be in flight and not a SCSI
command.

items.title: scsi: libiscsi: Validate the task named by a management response
items.summary:
In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

scsi: libiscsi: Validate the task named by a management response

__iscsi_complete_pdu() fetches the task for five response types from one
place and checks only that the index resolved:

      case ISCSI_OP_LOGOUT_RSP:
      case ISCSI_OP_LOGIN_RSP:
      case ISCSI_OP_TEXT_RSP:
      case ISCSI_OP_SCSI_TMFUNC_RSP:
      case ISCSI_OP_NOOP_IN:
              task = iscsi_itt_to_task(conn, hdr->itt);
              if (!task)
                      return ISCSI_ERR_BAD_ITT;

iscsi_itt_to_task() bounds the index against cmds_max and looks at
nothing else, so a target can name any slot in the pool, including one
that has never been used. task->conn is then NULL, and both
iscsi_nop_out_rsp() and iscsi_complete_task() dereference it. One
unsolicited NOP-In is enough; a Text Response carrying the same ITT
crashes in iscsi_complete_task() instead.

Require the task to be in flight and not a SCSI command, the way
iscsi_itt_to_ctask() does for the command opcodes.

items.title: mac802154: fix data race and NULL deref on local->assoc_dev
items.summary:
In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

mac802154: fix data race and NULL deref on local->assoc_dev

local->assoc_dev is shared between the association path and the
association-response worker without common synchronization.

mac802154_perform_association() stores the coordinator pointer and waits
for a response. Its timeout and error paths clear the pointer and return
to mac802154_associate(), which may then free the coordinator object.
Meanwhile, mac802154_rx_mac_cmd_worker() may observe the associating bit
and enter mac802154_process_association_resp(), which dereferences
assoc_dev.

The worker's bit test and the handler's pointer dereference are not
atomic with respect to cleanup. Cleanup can clear assoc_dev between them,
causing a NULL dereference, or free the coordinator while the response
handler still uses the pointer.

The recorded result is exposed to the same window. assoc_status and
assoc_addr are written by the handler but read by the association path
while the associating bit is still set, so a second response for the same
request - a malicious one, for instance - can replace them between those
reads and leave the caller with an incoherent status and address pair.

The response handler only needs the coordinator extended address.
Replace assoc_dev with a cached address, removing the pointer lifetime
dependency. Protect the cached address and the associating bit with a
dedicated spinlock. A READ_ONCE()/WRITE_ONCE() pair would not guarantee
an atomic __le64 access on all 32-bit architectures.

wpan_dev->association_lock cannot be reused here: nl802154_associate()
holds it across rdev_associate(), hence for the whole of
mac802154_perform_association() including the wait for the response.
A response handler taking that lock would only get it once the
association has already given up.

Reset the completion, publish the cached address, and set the associating
bit while holding the lock. The response handler takes the lock, rechecks
the bit and the cached address, records the response, clears the bit, and
only then completes the waiter. Thus cleanup cannot pass the handler
between its state check and completion, and the cached 64-bit value
cannot tear.

The handler clears the bit before completing, not the woken waiter:
otherwise complete() is issued under the lock and a second (e.g.
malicious) response can reacquire it before the waiter and replace the
result. So a wait that returns success implies the bit is already clear,
and the success and negative-response paths return directly. The
transmit-error and timeout paths still clear it under assoc_lock, which
serializes any racing response against the cleanup while the call returns
the error it already selected. Both paths snapshot assoc_status and
assoc_addr under the same lock.

Both users run in process context, so a plain spinlock is sufficient.
The lock is not held while waiting for the completion.

items.title: sctp: validate chunk length in the inqueue parser
items.summary:
In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

sctp: validate chunk length in the inqueue parser

SCTP chunks always include a four-byte generic header, but
sctp_inq_pop() currently accepts shorter declared lengths. A zero-length
chunk leaves chunk_end at the current header.

When ASCONF is covered by the association's SCTP-AUTH policy,
sctp_assoc_bh_rcv() can continue before the state machine performs its
normal chunk-length check. sctp_inq_pop() then returns the same malformed
chunk repeatedly and the receive softirq can lock up.

A remote SCTP peer can trigger this after establishing an association on
a kernel built with CONFIG_IP_SCTP and configured with
net.sctp.addip_enable=1 and net.sctp.auth_enable=1. The reproducer did
not require application credentials, a shared SCTP AUTH key, or
net.sctp.addip_noauth_enable=1.

On commit f967455fb2a5 ("seg6: reset IP6CB after IPv6 decapsulation"),
one zero-length ASCONF caused repeated
watchdog soft-lockup reports in a two-vCPU KVM guest. All 3 pre-trigger
health probes succeeded, while 36 of 37 post-trigger probes failed. With
this change, all 37 post-trigger probes succeeded and no equivalent
soft-lockup signature appeared.

Reject chunks shorter than the generic SCTP header at the shared inqueue
parser boundary. Mark the packet for discard before either caller can
continue processing it, while preserving the four-byte generic minimum.
Declared-length 1 through 4 controls and kernel-generated ASCONF traffic
remained healthy. The patched sctp_hello selftest passed for IPv4 and
IPv6.

The complete private reproducer and validation evidence are available
directly to maintainers on request.

items.title: KVM: x86/mmu: Cope with the SS bit being set in #NPF exit codes
items.summary:
In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

KVM: x86/mmu: Cope with the SS bit being set in #NPF exit codes

When running Hyper-V from Windows 11, KVM is seeing the SS bit set
in nested page fault error codes produced for shadowed NPT.  The AMD
manual is unclear about when SS is set, including whether it can be set
when SupervisorShadowStackEn (bit 6) is not set in the MISC_CTL field
of the VMCB.

Nevertheless, the unexpected SS bit causes out of bounds accesses in
permission_fault(), seen as either WARNs or UBSAN reports:

  kernel: UBSAN: array-index-out-of-bounds in arch/x86/kvm/mmu.h:225:27
  kernel: index 34 is out of range for type 'u16 [16]'

(in this case, the page fault error code is 34*2=0x44, i.e. SS|U; the
report shows SS|U|W happening as well).  Fix the handling of unknown
error codes by dropping SS and (with a WARN) any bits not among those
that permission_fault() expects to receive.

At the same time, given the uncertainty about when hardware sets SS,
follow the processor's behavior when constructing the fault's error
code, and preserve the SS bit as passed to FNAME(walk_addr_generic).
While the behavior is surprising, there's a possibility that Hyper-V
expects it (Hyper-V does not even enable CET unless it finds MBEC/GMET!),
so retain the information when reflecting the fault to L1 instead of
unconditionally discarding it.

Bisection shows that this started happening with commit 687ee95c1b6d ("KVM:
nSVM: enable GMET for guests"), even though SHSTK was available to guests
since Linux 6.18.  However, this is not because bit 1 of MISC_CTL (GMET)
somehow enables reporting the SS bit; rather, it's simply that Hyper-V
never uses CET unless GMET is also present.  The WARN is reproducible
even with gmet=0, with some hacking of kvm-unit-tests's cet.c testcase
to ensure that the first access to the shadow stack triggers a page fault.

items.title: net: psp: do not inherit the Rx association on clone
items.summary:
In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

net: psp: do not inherit the Rx association on clone

sk->psp_assoc sits past sk_dontcopy_end, so sock_copy() copies it into
every socket accepted from a listener without taking a reference, while
inet_sock_destruct() puts for every inet socket. psp_twsk_init() does
refcount_inc() for the timewait socket, so a child closing through
TIME_WAIT cancels its own put and leaves the association with one
reference and N timewait sockets holding the same pointer. Closing the
listener frees it, and the timewait timers then put freed memory.

Rejecting the association on a listening socket is not sufficient: a socket
can acquire one while established and then be turned back into a listener,
because tcp_disconnect() leaves sk->psp_assoc in place.

  BUG: KASAN: slab-use-after-free in psp_twsk_assoc_free+0x6f/0xf0
  Write of size 4 at addr ffff888110f9255c by task swapper/7/0
   psp_twsk_assoc_free+0x6f/0xf0
   inet_twsk_put+0xda/0x1b0
   call_timer_fn+0x53/0x2e0
   __run_timers+0x764/0xa80
  Freed by task 99:
   kfree+0x1a7/0x500
   process_one_work+0x7ec/0x1100

An association carries a per-connection SPI and key, so a child must not
inherit the parent's. Clear it on clone.

   kthread_worker_fn+0x1ff/0x790

Canceling the last inactive work skips pwq_dec_nr_active(), so an empty
pwq can remain on pending_pwqs when its refcnt reaches zero.
pwq_release_workfn() currently puts the pool before removing that pwq.

the pwq remains reachable, and node_activate_pending_pwq() may trylock
the freed pool->lock.

Remove the pwq from pending_pwqs before putting the pool.

items.title: FearlessCMS is a flat-file `content` management system centered on simplicity and open source. Prior to version 0.1.4, five debug/test PHP scripts under `admin/` perform privile...
items.summary: FearlessCMS is a flat-file `content` management system centered on simplicity and open source. Prior to version 0.1.4, five debug/test PHP scripts under `admin/` perform privileged operations without `isLoggedIn()` authentication checks, CSRF protection or adequate `path` validation. On PHP's built-in development server, including the default Docker deployment, `router.php` checks an unnormalized admin URI prefix while the filesystem resolves dot segments, so `/./admin/` bypasses the admin login gate and executes those scripts directly. In `admin/debug_save_flow.php`, attacker-controlled `path` and `content` reach `file_put_contents` for arbitrary `.md` writes under `content`/ or outside it through `path` traversal, enabling site defacement and stored JavaScript in public pages; `print_r($_POST)` output without `htmlspecialchars` escaping also causes reflected cross-site scripting. The `admin/debug_content.php` `path` parameter reaches `scandir()`, `file_get_contents()` and `posix_getpwuid()`, permitting arbitrary directory enumeration and `.md` file reads that expose absolute paths, ownership, permissions, hashes and `content` previews. The `admin/preview-handler.php` endpoint accepts JSON `content` and `title` and writes enumerable files under `content/_preview/`, enabling stored cross-site scripting and disk exhaustion. The `admin/testdebug.php` endpoint appends to `admin/testdebug.log` without authentication, also enabling disk exhaustion. The `admin/test_redirect.php` script exposes a test artifact but escapes its inputs and is not itself an XSS sink. Stored script execution can steal sessions and compromise administrators when they view affected `content`. Reads and writes execute with PHP's privileges; the tested deployment runs PHP as root, amplifying filesystem impact. This issue is fixed in version 0.1.4.

items.title: vLLM: DoS via unbounded chat_template Jinja2 rendering exhausts the renderer thread pool
items.summary:
### Summary
vLLM renders chat templates by passing the resolved Jinja2 source to `tokenizer.apply_chat_template()`, which compiles and `.render()`s it in an `ImmutableSandboxedEnvironment`. The sandbox prevents code-execution escapes but imposes **no wall-clock timeout, no output-size cap, and no nested-loop or binop limit**. The render runs in a `ThreadPoolExecutor` whose `max_workers` defaults to **1**, and CPython worker threads cannot be interrupted. An authenticated API client (or a malicious model repo loaded with `trust_remote_code=False`) can therefore submit a single short template and permanently wedge **all** chat-style endpoints (`/v1/chat/completions`, `/v1/responses`, `/tokenize`, `/pooling`-chat, `/invocations`-chat) for every tenant until the process is restarted. A string-multiplication variant instead OOM-kills the API-server process. Because of a separately-reported (GHSA-jmjw-q4x3-hmc2) gate omission on `/v1/responses`, the remote authenticated attacker vector works in **default `vllm serve` configuration** with no operator opt-in.

### Impact
A single authenticated request of <100 bytes permanently denies all chat-style inference (`/v1/chat/completions`, `/v1/responses`, `/tokenize`, `/pooling`-chat, `/invocations`-chat) to **every tenant** of the API-server replica until the operator restarts the process. The string-multiplication variant OOM-kills the process. In a multi-tenant deployment this is a cross-tenant denial-of-service from any one tenant. From the malicious-model angle, a model repo whose `tokenizer_config.json` carries the hostile template wedges every replica that loads it on the first legitimate chat request, with `trust_remote_code=False`.

**Preconditions:** any non-harmony model (`model_type != gpt_oss`); `renderer_num_workers` at its default of 1; for the default-config authenticated API attacker vector, `--chat-template` must be unset (the default because most HF models ship their own).
**Blast radius:** API-server process, per replica. Engine/worker processes unaffected by the CPU variant (event loop survives); affected by the memory variant (process OOM).
**Persistence:** until process restart. Survives client disconnect.

This advisory was fixed in [MR50300](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/50300).

items.title: Go JOSE: Panics in JSON parsing
items.summary:
### Summary

Parsing deeply nested JSON structures can hit Go's stack limit, causing the application to crash.

Note: this advisory is the same as https://github.com/go-jose/go-jose/security/advisories/GHSA-6mp9-8xrw-74r4.

### Impact

Denial of service vulnerability. Any application that parses untrusted JSON via go-jose is exposed.

### Workarounds

Reject large inputs before parsing them.

### Acknowledgements

Thanks to Dohyun Kim (@azza999), Joshua Rogers of AISLE Research, and Sueun Cho for alerting us to the need to patch this.

items.title: Tornado: Open redirect in RedirectHandler via protocol-relative URLs
items.summary:
### Summary

`tornado.web.RedirectHandler` builds its target URL by substituting parts of the request path into a template. Depending on where those substitutions appear in the template, an attacker can craft a request that redirects to a host of their choosing. This creates an open redirect on the application's domain, which can be used in phishing.

### Impact

Applications are affected if they use `RedirectHandler` with a URL template where a regex capture group can influence the scheme or host of the redirect. This includes:

- **A substitution at the start of the path**, for example `(r"/(.*)/target", RedirectHandler, {"url": "/{0}/destination"})`. A request to `https://example.com//evil.com/target` redirects to `//evil.com/destination`, a protocol-relative URL pointing to evil.com. Variants using backslashes or encoded characters have the same effect, because browsers treat them as equivalent to `//`.
- **A substitution directly after the host**, for example `(r"/old(.*)", RedirectHandler, {"url": "https://new.example.com{0}"})`. A request to `/old.evil.com/` or `/old@evil.com/` redirects to evil.com.
- **A template that begins with a substitution** (such as `"{0}"`), which can be given an absolute URL.

Applications are not affected if their `RedirectHandler` templates use only static URLs, or if every substitution comes after a fixed host and a `/` (for example `"/static/{0}"` or `"https://example.com/{0}"`). Other uses of `RequestHandler.redirect()` are not affected by this advisory, although applications that pass user-controlled input to `redirect()` should validate it themselves.

### Patches

Fixed in Tornado 6.6. `RedirectHandler` now returns a 400 error if the substituted values would change the scheme or host of the redirect from what the template specifies. As a result, substitutions can no longer be used in the scheme or host part of a template. The similar check in `StaticFileHandler` has also been hardened against backslash and whitespace variants.

### Workarounds

- Change `RedirectHandler` templates so every substitution comes after a fixed prefix ending in `/`, or write capture-group regexes that cannot match characters such as `/`, `\`, `@`, `.` or `:` where they could affect the host.
- Alternatively, replace `RedirectHandler` with a custom handler that validates the target before calling `self.redirect()`.

### Credit

Reported by Longwei Wang (@gn00295120).

items.title: Crass: Incorrect tokenization of bad URLs enables CSS sanitizer bypass
items.summary:
## Summary

Crass's tokenizer didn't terminate a bad URL token at a `)` that followed an escaped backslash (`\\`). As a result, Crass consumed more input as part of the bad URL than a spec-compliant browser does. CSS sanitizers that parse untrusted CSS with Crass and re-emit it could be tricked into passing through declarations, style rules, or at-rules (including `@import`) that the sanitizer would otherwise have removed, but that a browser would then parse and apply.

## Details

While consuming the remnants of a bad URL (CSS Syntax Level 3, §4.3.15), Crass checked whether the *previously consumed* code point and the next code point formed a valid escape, in addition to checking the next two unconsumed code points. After an escaped backslash, the previously consumed code point is a backslash, so a following `)` was incorrectly treated as escaped and the bad URL token continued until the next unescaped `)` or the end of the input.

Browsers terminate the bad URL at that `)`, so everything Crass treated as part of the bad URL is live CSS to a browser.

This bug has existed in every released version of Crass.

## Impact

Crass by itself only mis-tokenizes input. The security impact is on CSS sanitizers that use Crass to make allow/deny decisions and then re-serialize the CSS. Exploitation requires a sanitizer that doesn't reject bad URL tokens wherever they occur. Confirmed examples (verified in Chromium against the sanitizers' output):

- **Sanitize** (all versions through 7.0.0):
  - In `Sanitize::CSS.properties` and `style` attributes, a bad URL inside a `[...]` or `(...)` block in the value of an allowlisted property can smuggle arbitrary declarations, such as `position: fixed` or a `background-image` URL with a disallowed protocol.
  - In `Sanitize::CSS.stylesheet` and `<style>` elements, a bad URL in a selector can smuggle arbitrary style rules and at-rules, including `@import`.
- **Loofah** (`Loofah::HTML5::Scrub.scrub_css`, used for `style` attributes), and therefore **rails-html-sanitizer** (`sanitize_css`, and `sanitize` when `style` is a permitted attribute): a bad URL inside an allowlisted function such as `calc()` or `rgb()` can smuggle declarations Loofah normally strips, such as `position: fixed` and `url()` values.

Smuggled CSS can be used for UI redress (clickjacking or phishing overlays), loading attacker-controlled external resources, and, where rules or `@import` can be smuggled, CSS-based data exfiltration. This vulnerability doesn't allow script execution in modern browsers.

## Patches

Fixed in Crass 1.0.8. Users of Sanitize, Loofah, rails-html-sanitizer, or any other library that uses Crass to sanitize CSS should upgrade Crass to 1.0.8 or later.

## Workarounds

There are no practical workarounds other than upgrading. Rejecting any CSS input that contains the character sequence `\\` would block the known trigger, but this is a blunt measure and may reject legitimate CSS.

## References

- CSS Syntax Module Level 3, "Consume the remnants of a bad url": https://drafts.csswg.org/css-syntax-3/#consume-remnants-of-bad-url

items.title: Backstage catalog rules can be bypassed for URL locations using encoded path segments
items.summary:
## Summary

`@backstage/plugin-catalog-backend` matches URL-type locations against `catalog.rules` location patterns using the raw URL string submitted by the user, while URL readers resolve that same string in canonical form when fetching the location's content. A URL can therefore be crafted so that it appears to belong to a trusted location scope during rule evaluation, but is fetched from a different scope.

## Details

When a deployment restricts catalog kinds to trusted URL prefixes using `catalog.rules` location patterns, `DefaultCatalogRulesEnforcer` applies glob matching directly to the raw `location.target` string. The URL readers used for ingestion resolve the same target in canonical form, including normalizing percent-encoded dot segments. A registered location such as `https://<host>/trusted/%2e%2e/attacker/repo/blob/main/catalog-info.yaml` matches a `https://<host>/trusted/**` pattern as a raw string, but resolves to and is fetched from `https://<host>/attacker/repo/...` when its content is read.

An authenticated user with permission to register catalog locations (`catalog.location.create`) can use this to have an entity from an untrusted source admitted as if it originated from a trusted location scope.

## Impact

The crossed boundary is the operator-configured catalog ingestion policy: entity content from outside the trusted location scope is ingested as if it were within it. Downstream consequences depend on deployment configuration, for example actions taken with integration credentials by processors or scaffolder when acting on the ingested entity. The assessment of this report found no basis for impact claims beyond the ingestion policy boundary itself.

## Patches

This is fixed in `@backstage/plugin-catalog-backend` 3.9.2 (Backstage release 1.54.10) and 4.0.2 (Backstage release 1.56.1). Version 4.0.1 as published is not fixed.

## Workarounds

No complete workaround is available for deployments that rely on URL location patterns to restrict catalog kinds. Restricting location registration permissions reduces exposure.

items.title: In deployments of WSO2 Identity Server configured with a case-insensitive user store and a case...
items.summary:
In deployments of WSO2 Identity Server configured with a case-insensitive user store and a case-sensitive database for identity data, mismatches in username case handling can occur. This inconsistency results in OAuth token revocation operations failing to correctly identify usernames containing mixed-case characters during certain lifecycle events, preventing tokens from being invalidated.

A malicious actor can exploit this vulnerability by possessing a valid access or refresh token associated with a mixed-case username. In affected configurations, these tokens may not be revoked when expected. The actor can then leverage these unrevoked tokens, before their expiry, to continue performing actions that should have been restricted, effectively bypassing intended access controls.

items.title: Python Social Auth: OpenID Connect nonce is not bound to the browser session, so a stolen authorization code logs the attacker in as the victim
items.summary:
### Summary

The generic OpenID Connect backend (`OpenIdConnectAuth` and every backend built on it) stores the `nonce` in the shared Association table, not in the user's session. When the ID token comes back, `validate_claims` only checks that the nonce exists in that table and is not expired. It does not check that the nonce was issued to the browser that is finishing the login.

So the nonce does not do its job. OIDC Core (section 15.5.2) and RFC 9700 (section 4.5) use the nonce to stop authorization code injection: an attacker who gets hold of a victim's unused authorization code should not be able to redeem it in the attacker's own browser. With social-auth-core, the attacker can. They start their own login to get a valid `state` for their session, then hit the callback with the victim's `code` and their own `state`. `state` passes because it belongs to the attacker's session, and the nonce in the victim's ID token passes because it is in the global table. The attacker's browser is now logged in as the victim.

PKCE would block this, but `OpenIdConnectAuth` sets `DEFAULT_USE_PKCE = False` (the OAuth2 base class defaults to `True`), so the nonce is the only binding in the default setup.

### Tested versions

social-auth-core 6.1.1 (latest), 6.1.0 and 5.2.0, with social-auth-app-django 7.1.0 and Django 6.1.2, Python 3.14. The same code is on master (098ef399c1).

### Details

`social_core/backends/open_id_connect.py` in 6.1.1:

- line 252: `auth_params` calls `get_and_store_nonce(self.authorization_url(), state)`
- lines 333 to 346: `get_and_store_nonce` stores the nonce as an `OpenIdConnectAssociation` keyed by `server_url` and `handle=nonce`. The state goes into `assoc_type` but is never read back.
- lines 348 to 358: `get_nonce` looks the nonce up by `server_url` and `handle` only
- lines 393 to 415: `validate_claims` accepts any stored, unexpired nonce and removes it
- line 110: `DEFAULT_USE_PKCE = False`

### PoC

Everything runs locally. `mockidp.py` is a small OpenID provider on 127.0.0.1 that checks `redirect_uri` and enforces PKCE when a `code_challenge` was sent, like a normal provider. `social_nonce.py` uses two Django test clients as two browsers.

```
pip install social-auth-core social-auth-app-django django pyjwt cryptography
python social_nonce.py
```

Output on 6.1.1:

```
[inject] attacker session completes with victim code: (200, 'user=victim')
```

Controls:

```
MODE=control_victim python social_nonce.py
[control] victim completes normally: (200, 'user=victim')

MODE=control_unknown_nonce python social_nonce.py
[control] unknown nonce: ('EXC', 'AuthResponseError: The authentication response could not be matched to the request.')

PKCE=1 python social_nonce.py
[inject] attacker session completes with victim code: ('EXC', 'AuthCredentialError: The authorization code was rejected. Please restart login.')
```

So the nonce check runs, but it accepts a nonce that belongs to another browser. With PKCE on, the same attack fails.

import json, time, secrets, threading, hashlib, base64, urllib.parse
from http.server import BaseHTTPRequestHandler, ThreadingHTTPServer
import jwt
from cryptography.hazmat.primitives.asymmetric import rsa

def b64u(b): return base64.urlsafe_b64encode(b).rstrip(b"=").decode()

class IdP:
    def __init__(self, port=0, client_id="rp-client", client_secret="rp-secret", name="idp"):
        self.key = rsa.generate_private_key(public_exponent=65537, key_size=2048)
        self.kid = name + "-k1"
        self.client_id, self.client_secret = client_id, client_secret
        self.codes = {}
        self.access = {}
        self.claims_override = {}
        self.srv = ThreadingHTTPServer(("127.0.0.1", port), self._handler())
        self.port = self.srv.server_address[1]
        self.issuer = f"http://127.0.0.1:{self.port}"
        threading.Thread(target=self.srv.serve_forever, daemon=True).start

items.summary:
## Summary

Any vLLM deployment serving a model of the DeepSeek-OCR family — `deepseek-ai/DeepSeek-OCR`, `deepseek-ai/DeepSeek-OCR-2`, or `baidu/Unlimited-OCR` (whose `UnlimitedOCRForCausalLM` subclasses `DeepseekOCRForCausalLM`) — can be **killed by a single unauthenticated chat request carrying an ordinary, schema-valid PNG image**, under completely default server configuration.

The image model's input validation contains a guard inherited from the upstream DeepSeek-OCR reference implementation:

```python
# vllm/model_executor/models/deepseek_ocr.py:478-479  (_parse_and_validate_image_input)
if torch.sum(pixel_values).item() == 0:
    return None
```

In the original research code this was an empty-batch shortcut; in vLLM's serving architecture `pixel_values` is the actual client image tensor, and the condition is **exactly satisfiable by a legitimate image**: the in-tree `DeepseekOCRProcessor` normalizes pixels with `ToTensor + Normalize(0.5, 0.5)` (`vllm/transformers_utils/processors/deepseek_ocr.py:120-140`), mapping pixel value 0 → exactly −1.0 and 255 → exactly +1.0 in float32. A 1024×1024 image that is half pure black and half pure white (a perfectly ordinary 1-bit-style scanned-document PNG for an OCR model) therefore yields `torch.sum(pixel_values) == 0.0` **exactly** (equal counts of ±1.0; pairwise reduction stays integer-exact, well inside float32's 2²⁴ exactness bound). `ImageOps.pad(image, (1024, 1024))` is the identity map for an already-1024×1024 image (`processors/deepseek_ocr.py:350-355`), so no padding pixels disturb the balance.

Returning `None` makes `embed_multimodal` return `None` (`deepseek_ocr.py:606-611`), which immediately trips the engine-side sanity check in the worker:

```python
# vllm/v1/worker/utils.py:512  (sanity_check_mm_encoder_outputs)
assert isinstance(mm_embeddings, (list, tuple, torch.Tensor)), (
    "Expected multimodal embeddings to be a list/tuple of 2D tensors, ...")
```

The `AssertionError` is raised inside the encoder runner of the EngineCore worker process with no per-request containment, escapes to the busy loop's top-level handler (`vllm/v1/engine/core.py:1368`, "EngineCore encountered a fatal error."), triggers `EngineDeadError` at the API server (`vllm/v1/engine/async_llm.py:843`), and the whole process tree shuts down permanently. `/health` refuses connections until a manual restart.

Verified end-to-end on the official `vllm/vllm-openai:v0.30.0` image (id d076d77d8dad) with real `deepseek-ai/DeepSeek-OCR` weights: after confirming `/health` 200, a text chat 200, and two control images (all-white and all-black 1024×1024) 200, the single half-black/half-white request returned HTTP 500 (`EngineCore encountered an issue`), the engine log shows `AssertionError: Expected multimodal embeddings to be a list/tuple of 2D tensors ... got <class 'NoneType'>` at `v1/worker/utils.py:512`, the API server shut itself down, and the container exited (`Exited (0)`, `OOMKilled=false`). Every subsequent request, including `GET /health`, fails at the socket. The vulnerable check is unchanged on `main` (verified 2026-09-30 against the raw file on the default branch).

**Environment notes (disclosed for completeness; unrelated to the sink):** (1) the v0.30.0 image's Triton version refuses to compile `deepencoder.py`'s fused rel-pos attention kernel (`LOG2E` non-constexpr global) during the startup profile run; per the compiler's own suggestion we set `TRITON_ALLOW_NON_CONSTEXPR_GLOBALS=1` — an environment workaround only, no source file was modified. (2) DeepSeek-OCR ships no `chat_template`, so verification passed a one-line `--chat-template` that concatenates message content text; this does not touch the image data path. (3) The zero-sum check aggregates over the whole per-step modality batch, so the trigger image must be alone in its encoder batch — trivially true on an idle instance (our verification: first attempt, single request), and simply retried otherwise.

items.title: vLLM: Public multimodal SHM handle forgery reaches worker-side `pickle.loads()` with insecure serialization disabled
items.summary:
## Affected

- **Ecosystem / package:** pip / `vllm`
- **Affected versions:** vLLM < 0.32.0.

## Summary

When `--mm-processor-cache-type shm` is enabled, vLLM's multimodal SHM cache represents a cached item with an `address` and `monotonic_id` pair and treats that pair as authority to dereference shared memory in the worker. A public scale-out request can supply its own multimodal `features.kwargs_data`, so an authenticated caller can forge an inner SHM carrier that points at attacker-controlled bytes already staged in the ring buffer. The worker then reaches `pickle.loads()` while deserializing the forged object.

This is reachable through ordinary public HTTP routes and does not require `VLLM_ALLOW_INSECURE_SERIALIZATION=1`. The live chain used `/v1/chat/completions/render` to obtain a valid feature envelope, `/v1/chat/completions` to stage attacker-chosen bytes into SHM, and `/inference/v1/generate` to submit the forged inner carrier.

## Affected code

Links pinned to the confirmed commit [`752a3a504485`](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/tree/752a3a504485790a2e8491cacbb35c137339ad34) (v0.25.1):

- [`vllm/distributed/device_communicators/shm_object_storage.py#L375-L400`](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/blob/752a3a504485790a2e8491cacbb35c137339ad34/vllm/distributed/device_communicators/shm_object_storage.py#L375-L400) — SHM object deserialization reaches `pickle.loads(serialized_data)` for byte objects.
- [`vllm/multimodal/cache.py#L567-L581`](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/blob/752a3a504485790a2e8491cacbb35c137339ad34/vllm/multimodal/cache.py#L567-L581) — sender emits an SHM carrier containing only `address` and `monotonic_id`.
- [`vllm/multimodal/cache.py#L711-L737`](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/blob/752a3a504485790a2e8491cacbb35c137339ad34/vllm/multimodal/cache.py#L711-L737) — worker dereferences the untrusted pair and reads the SHM object.
- [`vllm/entrypoints/scale_out/token_in_token_out/serving.py#L146-L173`](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/blob/752a3a504485790a2e8491cacbb35c137339ad34/vllm/entrypoints/scale_out/token_in_token_out/serving.py#L146-L173) — public `features.kwargs_data` is decoded into engine input without authenticating SHM handles before handoff.

The public scale-out route decodes attacker-controlled `features.kwargs_data` into `MultiModalKwargsItem`s and hands them straight to the engine — no authentication of the SHM handle:

```python
# vllm/entrypoints/scale_out/token_in_token_out/serving.py Lines 155-165
            # Deserialize tensor data when present; None → cache hit.
            mm_kwargs: dict[str, list[MultiModalKwargsItem | None]] = {}
            if features.kwargs_data is not None:
                for modality, items in features.kwargs_data.items():
                    mm_kwargs[modality] = [
                        decode_mm_kwargs_item(item) if item is not None else None
                        for item in items
                    ]
            else:
                for modality, hashes in features.mm_hashes.items():
                    mm_kwargs[modality] = [None] * len(hashes)
```

In the worker, a decoded item that carries an `address` is treated as authority to dereference shared memory: the `(address, monotonic_id)` pair alone drives the read, with no binding to the cache key or to who issued the handle:

```python
# vllm/multimodal/cache.py Lines 711-723
    @override
    def get_and_update_item(
        self,
        mm_item: MultiModalKwargsItem | None,
        mm_hash: str,
    ) -> MultiModalKwargsItem:
        assert mm_item is not None, f"Expected an address item for {mm_hash=}"
        if "address" in mm_item:
            address = cast(int, mm_item["address"].data)
            monotonic_id = cast(int, mm_item["monotonic_id"].data)
            return self._shm_cache.get(address, monotonic_id)

        return mm_item
```

The dereference lands in the SHM deserializer, which `pickle.loads()` any chunk tagged as `bytes` — so attacker bytes stage

items.title: vLLM: Out-of-vocabulary prompt token id passes input validation and triggers a CUDA device-side assert (engine crash / DoS)
items.summary:
For a model whose vocabulary size is an exact multiple of the embedding padding size (64) — e.g. any Llama-2-family model, vocab 32000 — a single request carrying a pre-tokenized prompt with token id equal to the vocab size (32000) passes vLLM's input-id validation but is one past the last embedding row. At tensor-parallel size 1 the embedding lookup does not mask indices, so the id reaches `F.embedding` out of range and raises a CUDA device-side assert, which poisons the engine's CUDA context and takes the engine down. Any client that can send pre-tokenized input (`/v1/completions` with `prompt` as token ids, `/tokenize`-fed flows, or the `kv_transfer_params["prompt_token_ids"]` reuse path) can trigger it.

## Root cause
`vllm/v1/engine/input_processor.py` accepts a token id when `id <= max(tokenizer.max_token_id, model_config.get_vocab_size() - 1)`.
`vllm/tokenizers/hf.py` computes `max_token_id = max(max(vocab.values()), tokenizer.vocab_size)`. For Llama-2 tokenizers `max(vocab.values()) = 31999` but `tokenizer.vocab_size = 32000`, so `max_token_id = 32000` — one greater than the largest valid id.
The engine bound therefore becomes `max(32000, 31999) = 32000`, and id 32000 is accepted.
The model's embedding has `pad_vocab_size(32000, 64) = 32000` rows (no padding), valid indices 0..31999. At `VocabParallelEmbedding.forward` with `tp_size == 1` there is no masking, so index 32000 hits `F.embedding` out of range.

## Affected
- tp=1 (single GPU per model — common per-copy layout). tp>1 masks via `get_masked_input_and_mask`, so the id is clamped, not an OOB — likely wrong output rather than a crash.
- Models whose vocab is a multiple of 64 with `tokenizer.vocab_size` one past the max real id (Llama-2 family, vocab 32000, is the clear case). Qwen2.5 is NOT affected (padded headroom).

## Suggested fix 
max_token_id in vllm/tokenizers/hf.py now uses tokenizer.vocab_size - 1, so an id equal to the vocabulary size fails input validation instead of reaching the embedding. Fixed in [MR59491](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/59491), released in v0.32.0.

## Reporter
Shijie Lyu (GitHub shijie-lyu lshjhf@gmail.com). Reported privately per SECURITY.

This advisory was fixed in [MR59491](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/59491).

items.title: Wasmtime: Cranelift backend on aarch64 can jump to incorrect target on large Wasm `br_table` instruction
items.summary:
## Summary

When running with the Cranelift compiler backend on an aarch64 target, Wasmtime can compile a Wasm module with more than ~256k targets on one `br_table` instruction in a way that results in an incorrect conditional branch target. This conditional branch could then jump to arbitrary other code (at an user-controlled offset), leading to arbitrary sandbox escapes.

## Impact

Any Wasmtime engine running on aarch64 with default settings can be forced to jump to arbitrary code by a user-controlled Wasm module. All versions of Wasmtime/Cranelift that support aarch64, since the initial release of that support in 2020 (before Wasmtime v1.0), are affected.

## Patches

Wasmtime v36.0.19, v48.0.7, and v49.0.4 have been released which all fix this issue.

items.title: Measuring Users' Security and Privacy Concerns About Third-Party Community Bots on Discord
items.summary: Third-party community-based bots are central to how social platforms such as Discord work. They moderate content, manage roles, play music, and support AI-assisted conversations across millions of servers. Yet when a bot is installed in a server, it can access messages, user profiles, and server metadata concerning members who did not participate in the installation decision, with no standardized way to communicate the associated security and privacy implications. In this paper, we analyze 23,102 third-party Discord bots and 183,142 user reviews spanning 49 detected languages and five years of feedback (2021-2026). We employ LLM-based knowledge distillation and fine-tune a DeBERTa-based classifier to identify candidate security and privacy (S&P)-relevant reviews. After manually validating the complete classifier-positive set, we retain 8,832 reviews identified as S&P-relevant, representing an observed pipeline yield of 4.82%, and map them to a 31-theme S&P taxonomy extending prior work. Our results show that S&P-related reviews focus heavily on Data Sharing (30.5%) and Data Collection (16.2%). Confession and anonymity bots have pipeline-identified SPRRs above 50%, more than ten times the ecosystem-wide pipeline yield of 4.82%. Star ratings may obscure the frequency and valence of S&P-related discussion, while conventional metadata features, such as permission count and administrator status, show only weak associations with user-reported S&P concerns. We then build BotLens, a proof-of-concept auditing framework that combines review-derived S&P signals with bot metadata to provide on-demand decision support for the community-based bot ecosystem. BotLens exposes six tools through a Model Context Protocol server, supporting bot-level checkups, server-wide comparison, and integration with AI agents.

items.title: SpecGuard: Detecting Multi-Turn LLM Jailbreaks via Specification-Based Runtime Monitoring
items.summary: Multi-turn jailbreaks turn dialogue safety into a trace property: a violation may become identifiable only when user intent and assistant behavior are considered across multiple turns. Existing guard models largely classify individual messages or exchanges and return risk scores or labels, without executable safety semantics or a formally checkable decision trail. We present SpecGuard, a training-free, specification-driven framework for monitoring multi-turn LLM interactions. SpecGuard uses a fixed atomic-proposition contract to map natural-language observations into causally scoped, evidence-backed facts, and expresses forbidden interaction patterns as Linear Temporal Logic specifications. Each specification is compiled into a symbolic finite automaton that incrementally consumes the resulting dialogue trace. The same monitoring mechanism supports buffered runtime checking and retrospective auditing, while accepting runs produce replayable witnesses that identify the triggered specification, supporting facts, and relevant dialogue turns. Experiments on multi-turn safety benchmarks show that SpecGuard consistently outperforms representative open-source guard models while maintaining controlled false-positive rates. items.title: CoSA: The Conflict of Skills Attack in Real-World LLM Agent Ecosystems
items.summary: Agent Skills allow LLM agents to combine reusable capabilities, but checking each Skill in isolation cannot rule out policy violations when they are composed. We term such failures Conflict of Skills (CoS): artifacts or assessment signals produced for one purpose may be reused downstream without preserving the restrictions or authorization needed for their new use. Using controlled executions of publicly available Skills and matched single-Skill controls, we identify four recurring mechanisms behind CoS. Building on these findings, we introduce the Conflict of Skills Attack (CoSA), which adds locally admitted Skills to an existing pool to supply missing business operations (capability supplementation) or reshape artifact exchange, decision reuse, and target/action bindings (relationship reshaping). CoSA leaves existing Skills and runtime permissions unchanged. To evaluate this threat under autonomous Skill selection, we introduce CoSA-Bench, built from real-world Skills and controlled services, with 288 tasks across recruiting, finance, IT, and business, covering data leakage, unauthorized state modification, and unsafe execution. Across five LLMs and three agent harnesses, additions capped at 5% of each original pool raise the policy-violation rate from 35.02% to 58.45%, an increase of 23.43 percentage points. Trace analysis links compliant-to-violating transitions to cross-Skill dependencies involving the additions. Finally, we develop a lightweight harness-level guard that checks information flow and authorization before consequential actions. On OpenClaw recruiting tasks across five models, the guard reduces violations from 65.28% to 6.67%, while policy-compliant task completion on matched benign controls changes from 66.67% to 65.00%.

items.title: LLM WikiLeaks: Uncovering URL-Based Capability Extension and Security Circumvention in Agentic Message Boards
items.summary: Autonomous agents have been observed acting beyond their assigned tasks, accessing unauthorized systems, and establishing communication channels to exchange information, yet the Web and network-level techniques they use to extend their capabilities and circumvent security restrictions remain poorly understood. We study these techniques through the ProWiki incident, in which agents restricted to outbound HTTP GET requests repurposed a public German-language wiki as a message board. We analyze 14,591 agent edits containing 79,541 URL postings and present corroborating evidence that the published URLs reflect the agents' operational activity. We find that 26,717 URL occurrences (33.6%) embed target URLs within one to five layers of third-party Web services. By recursively reconstructing these nested URLs, we identify 67 distinct intermediate services and classify their functionality. Most intermediate layers (73.8%) extend agents' capabilities by delegating content extraction and transformation to external Web services: Markdown and OCR services convert web content into machine-readable text, JSON filtering services extract selected fields, and archival services expose historical versions of pages. The remaining 26.2% facilitate circumvention of access restrictions and evasion of detection, including CORS and fetch proxies that retrieve content on agents' behalf, and link shorteners and redirectors that hide destination URLs from mechanisms inspecting literal URLs or outer hostnames. Agents also reach the same targets through multiple URL paths, consistent with attempts to evade rate limits or obscure request origins. Our results expose a gap between the capabilities granted to agents and those they can obtain by composing publicly available Web services: restricting an agent's local toolset or direct Internet access may be insufficient while third-party services remain reachable.

items.title: Factual Yet One-Sided: Stance Poisoning and Evidence Balancing in Retrieval-Augmented Generation
items.summary: The stance expressed in responses from retrieval-augmented generation systems is significantly influenced by the stance distribution of the retrieved materials. Existing research on knowledge poisoning has primarily targeted factual errors. In contrast, this study focuses on injection attacks in which the facts are correct but the stance on a controversial issue is one-sided. At a mean topic-level poisoning share of 18.9% within the post-injection ProCon documents, all four generation models from different vendors exhibited stance shifts aligned with the poisoning direction; across four concentration levels, the shifts increased monotonically. This paper proposes a Stance-Balancing Middleware positioned between the retriever and the generator. It consists of stance detection, fixed balancing (2 supporting + 2 opposing + 1 neutral), and a debiasing prompt, without introducing additional large language model calls. Across all eight concentration-direction settings, the complete method reduced the magnitude of stance deviation by an estimated 0.106 to 0.350; the six settings at poisoning shares of 11.9%-18.9% remained significant after Holm adjustment (adjusted p <= 0.009). In the cross-model experiment, all eight model-direction combinations moved along the stance axis in the corrective direction, and seven of eight showed a clearly detected reduction in absolute distance from 0. In the concentration sweep, the post-defense intervals included 0 in all eight settings, while the cross-model pro-poisoning results retained small positive residual point estimates of +0.045 to +0.063. For 20 candidate documents, stance detection took approximately 1.5% of the median generation time on a single GPU and approximately 16% on CPU.

items.title: Waline login accepts a non-string email as a match-all MongoDB query
items.summary:
## Summary

The login endpoint POST /api/token reads the `email` field from the request body without checking its type and passes it straight into the MongoDB storage query. When `email` is not a string (for example a JSON object such as {"$ne": null}), the MongoDB storage adapter's parseWhere silently DROPS the field rather than rejecting the request, producing an empty filter that matches ALL users. The endpoint then verifies the submitted password against the FIRST user returned (user[0]), which in Waline is the first-registered user — the site administrator.

This is a PARTIAL authentication bypass, not a full one. The attacker still needs a valid password for that first user; this is not a zero-knowledge bypass and it does not disclose passwords. Its concrete effects are: (1) the email/identifier factor is removed for the administrator account, (2) user enumeration (a non-string email never fails the "no such user" branch), and (3) credential-stuffing amplification — an attacker can test a leaked or weak password against the administrator account without knowing the administrator's email.

## Details

Untyped input — packages/server/src/controller/token.js:17-18:
```
    const { email, password, code } = this.post();
    const user = await this.modelInstance.select({ email });
````
`email` comes from the request body with no type check.

The storage adapter silently drops a non-string key — packages/server/src/service/storage/mongodb.js, parseWhere():
```
    if (think.isString(where[k])) { filter[parseKey(k)] = { $eq: ... }; continue; }   // intended guard
    if (where[k] === undefined) { ... }
    if (Array.isArray(where[k]) && where[k][0]) { ... operator handling (IN/LIKE/!=/> ...) }
```
A plain object such as {"$ne": null} is neither a string, undefined, nor an array, so NONE of the branches run and nothing is added to `filter` for `email`. The result is filter = {} -> instance.where({}) -> MongoDB find({}) returns every user. (The array form, e.g. ["!=", ""], is a genuine operator injection that reaches $ne with the same match-all effect.)

First user is selected — token.js:22-26:
```
    if (think.isEmpty(user) || isVerifyUser || isBannedUser) { return this.fail(); }   // match-all -> not empty -> passes
    const checkPassword = this.checkPassword(password, user[0].password);
```
user[0] is the first record in MongoDB natural (insertion) order, i.e. the earliest-registered user, which in Waline is the administrator.

No upstream type validation — packages/server/src/logic/token.js:37-38:
```
    async postAction() { await this.useCaptchaCheck(); }
```
The only pre-check is the captcha; there is no isString(email/password) validation.

## Proof of Concept

Send a login request whose email is a non-string value:
```
    POST /api/token  HTTP/1.1
    Content-Type: application/json

    {"email": {"$ne": null}, "password": "<password-to-test>"}
```
- Because `email` is not a string, parseWhere adds nothing for it, so the query filter is {} and MongoDB returns all users.
- user[0] — the first-registered user, i.e. the administrator — is selected, and the submitted password is checked against the administrator's hash.
- If the password matches (for example via credential stuffing or a known/weak password), the attacker is authenticated as the administrator without ever knowing the administrator's email.
- Even when the password does not match, the request confirms that users exist (enumeration) and that the email factor is bypassable.

## Impact

An unauthenticated attacker can bypass the email/identifier factor of authentication for the first-registered user (the administrator) and have an arbitrary password checked directly against that account. This:
- enables user enumeration;
- amplifies credential stuffing against the administrator (no need to know the admin email — a leaked or weak password can be tested directly);

items.title: Vue I18n: `escapeParameter` does not escape named values when the same call also passes a list
items.summary: Vue I18n is the internationalization plugin for Vue.js. From 9.0.0-beta.5 until 11.4.14 and 12.0.0-alpha.5, enabling escapeParameter, called escapeParameterHtml in the Legacy API, does not escape named interpolation values when the same translation call supplies both list and named values because escapeParams() processes only the list branch. Applications that render translations as HTML and pass untrusted named values with a list can insert attacker-controlled markup, including phishing links, forms, and layout changes, and can permit script execution when combined with the srcdoc sanitizer bypass or on releases without the sanitizer. This issue is fixed in versions 11.4.14 and 12.0.0-alpha.5.

items.title: Highcharts Dashboards / Grid Pro: `DataTable.setCell` and column writers treat `__proto__` as an existing column.
items.summary: Highcharts JS is a JavaScript charting library based on SVG. From 1.0.0 until Dashboards 4.2.2, and from 2.0.0 until Grid Pro 3.2.0, Highcharts DataTable single-cell writers use an untrusted column ID as a key without rejecting __proto__ or constructor. DataTable.setCell, including Dashboards connector write-back and Grid Pro editing paths, can therefore write integer-indexed values onto Object.prototype or the Object constructor. In Dashboards releases with column aliases, a literal __proto__ ID is redirected by the alias map, while an alias targeting __proto__ reaches the unsafe write; later releases without aliases accept the unsafe ID directly. Those inherited values affect array and object reads and for-in enumeration throughout the page, which can alter application control flow or disrupt rendering. Exploitation requires control of the table or component column ID and a cell, point, or API write. This issue is fixed in Dashboards 4.2.2 and Grid Pro 3.2.0.

Styled-mode charts do not apply this option and are not affected. This issue is fixed in 11.4.9, 12.6.1 and 13.1.0.

items.title: Highcharts Core: AST `DOMParser` fallback assigns unsanitized markup to `innerHTML` during print
items.summary: Highcharts JS is a JavaScript charting library based on SVG. From 12.0.0 until 12.6.1 and 13.1.0, Highcharts falls back to assigning raw markup to innerHTML when DOMParser cannot return a document, before its allow-list is applied. In Chromium, the Trusted Types callback can throw while a beforeprint handler runs, so a page that redraws a chart during beforeprint can insert untrusted HTML text options into the hosting document. Event handlers in that markup then run in the page origin when printing begins. The issue affects HTML-rendered titles, labels, data labels, responsive text, and the Stock, Maps, and Gantt products shipped in the same package. This issue is fixed in 12.6.1 and 13.1.0.

items.title: HTTP::Body versions before 1.24_01 for Perl allow memory exhaustion via unbounded buffering of chunked request bodies
items.summary:
HTTP::Body versions before 1.24_01 for Perl allow memory exhaustion via unbounded buffering of chunked request bodies.

In chunked mode, used when no content length is given, add() holds each chunk in memory until all of it has arrived. A line that is not a chunk-size line, a size line without CRLF, or a size too large to fit an integer leaves the parser waiting forever, and every later add() grows the buffer.

A remote attacker can exhaust memory in applications that pass chunked request bodies to HTTP::Body.

items.title: HTTP::Body versions before 1.24_01 for Perl allow CPU exhaustion via regex backtracking on the filename of a multipart upload
items.summary:
HTTP::Body versions before 1.24_01 for Perl allow CPU exhaustion via regex backtracking on the filename of a multipart upload.

For every file part, the multipart parser finds the suffix of the uploaded filename by matching the default $basename_regexp, qr/[^.]+(\.[^\\\/]+)$/, against the whole basename. A basename made of many dots and ending in a backslash makes the regex backtrack in time quadratic in its length.

A remote attacker can exhaust CPU with one request, as a basename of about 32 KB takes several seconds to match and every file part is matched separately.
