items.summary: Asterisk is an open source private branch exchange and telephony toolkit. Prior to Asterisk 20.20.1, 21.12.3, 22.10.1, 23.4.1 and Certified Asterisk 22.8-cert3, an authenticated attacker with read-only permissions for the `Asterisk REST Interface (ARI)` may, under certain conditions, execute write operations through `REST-over-WebSocket`. The authorization bypass permits `arbitrary module path` loading and conditional remote code execution. The Asterisk HTTP web server must be enabled and reachable, and the attacker must already have valid `read-only ARI credentials`. HTTP is disabled by default and binds only to 127.0.0.1 by default even when enabled. This issue is fixed in Asterisk 20.20.1, 21.12.3, 22.10.1, 23.4.1 and Certified Asterisk 22.8-cert3.

The attacker must be able to connect to the `HTTP` server, which binds only to `127.0.0.1` by default even when enabled. This issue is fixed in Asterisk 20.20.1, 21.12.3, 22.10.1, 23.4.1 and Certified Asterisk 20.7-cert11, 22.8-cert3.

items.title: The Bot for Telegram on WooCommerce plugin for WordPress is vulnerable to Authentication Bypass leading to Account Takeover in all versions up to, and including, 1.3.0. The `/wp...
items.summary: The Bot for Telegram on WooCommerce plugin for WordPress is vulnerable to Authentication Bypass leading to Account Takeover in all versions up to, and including, 1.3.0. The `/wp-json/woo-telegram/v1/main/` REST endpoint is registered with `permission_callback => '__return_true'` and performs no Telegram webhook signature verification, allowing an unauthenticated attacker to POST a forged bot update with a `message.chat.id` set to any WordPress login name; `bftow_get_user_system_id()` resolves this attacker-supplied value to the targeted account via `get_user_by('login', $tgId)` with no ownership proof, and writes a login token computed as `md5($_SERVER['HTTP_USER_AGENT'] . time())` — both inputs are fully attacker-controlled or bounded within seconds using the response's own `Date` header. The resulting token is redeemable at the unauthenticated, capability-check-free, and nonce-less `?action=bftow_create_order&bftow_token=` endpoint, which calls `wp_set_auth_cookie()` unconditionally via `login_user_by_id`, issuing a persistent authenticated session cookie for the targeted account to the attacker. This makes it possible for unauthenticated attackers to log in as any WordPress user, including administrators, given only that user's username.

items.title: AVideo is a video-sharing Platform. Prior to 8.1.0, the live-streaming endpoint `view/videosListToLive.php` accepts an attacker-named streamer in `webSiteRootURL`, calls `Login:...
items.summary: AVideo is a video-sharing Platform. Prior to 8.1.0, the live-streaming endpoint `view/videosListToLive.php` accepts an attacker-named streamer in `webSiteRootURL`, calls `Login::run` in `objects/Login.php`, and trusts the returned JSON as session state. An unauthenticated remote attacker who can host an HTTP service reachable by the encoder can self-grant `isLogged` and `canStream` without legitimate credentials. The endpoint requires only nonempty `playlists_id` and `APISecret` values; `APISecret` is forwarded rather than checked against a stored secret. This path never calls `Streamer::isURLAllowed` and therefore works regardless of the operator's streamer allowlist. It fetches a second attacker-controlled video-list response and interpolates `videos[].path` without shell argument escaping into `ffprobe` and `ffmpeg` commands passed to `exec`; `isAudio` calls `isVideo` to reach the `ffprobe` command. Paths containing shell delimiters execute arbitrary operating-system commands as the web-server user. The request filter does not inspect the video-list JSON. This can disclose database and stored streamer credentials, compromise the upstream platform using those credentials, modify files owned by the web-server user, establish persistence, and deny encoder service. This issue is fixed in version 8.1.0.

items.title: AVideo is a video-sharing Platform. Prior to 8.1.0, the unauthenticated installer endpoint `install/checkConfiguration.php` assembles `videos/configuration.php` by interpolating...
items.summary: AVideo is a video-sharing Platform. Prior to 8.1.0, the unauthenticated installer endpoint `install/checkConfiguration.php` assembles `videos/configuration.php` by interpolating request parameters, including `webSiteRootURL`, into single-quoted PHP string literals without escaping. An attacker can terminate a literal and inject PHP that executes as the web-server user when the generated, directly requestable file is loaded. Exploitation requires `videos/configuration.php` to be absent, as on every fresh deployment or after the file is removed or moved; an existing file blocks this endpoint. The supplied `systemRootPath` must contain index.php and a connection using `databaseHost`, `databaseUser`, and `databasePass` must succeed, but the attacker can point those parameters to their own database server and needs no target credentials. The write location is also derived from `systemRootPath` without a base-directory constraint. This permits arbitrary command execution, reading and overwriting files owned by the web-server user, persistent PHP code, and control over stored database connection settings. The endpoint additionally interpolates request values into streamer and configuration INSERT statements, creating a secondary SQL-injection sink. This issue is fixed in version 8.1.0.

items.title: XWiki Remote Macros provides XWiki rendering macros that are useful when migrating content from Confluence. From 1.13 until 1.14.5, the `excerpt-include` macro does not properly...
items.summary: XWiki Remote Macros provides XWiki rendering macros that are useful when migrating content from Confluence. From 1.13 until 1.14.5, the `excerpt-include` macro does not properly escape the included page's title and executes `excerpt` content with the macro's rights. The title handling in `xwiki-pro-macros-ui/src/main/resources/Confluence/Macros/ExcerptInclude.xml` and the rendering of `excerpt` content into XWiki syntax both allow syntax injection. Any user able to edit a page, even without script or programming rights, can supply executable macro syntax in the title or `excerpt` and cause remote code execution when the page is included. This affects confidentiality, integrity and availability of the whole XWiki installation. This issue is fixed in version 1.14.5.

items.summary: The Contact Manager plugin for WordPress is vulnerable to Arbitrary File Upload in all versions up to, and including, 9.1.2 via the add_message function. This is due to an incomplete extension blacklist that fails to detect dangerous extensions when a trailing dot causes the extension-derivation routine to return an empty string, which sanitize_file_name() then silently removes before the file is written to disk. This makes it possible for unauthenticated attackers to upload files that may be executable, which makes remote code execution possible. Successful code execution additionally requires the server to use Apache with libapache2-mod-php (which maps .phar to PHP by default) and the attacker to retrieve the uploaded file within the brief window before it is removed by unlink() at end of request.

The server returns the generated destination filename in the response, giving the attacker the exact path needed to trigger the uploaded file.

items.summary: The Jupiter X Core plugin for WordPress is vulnerable to Authentication Bypass via the Twitter/X Social Login handler in all versions up to and including 4.61.0. The vulnerability exists within the verify_twitter_callback function because after exchanging the visitor's oauth_verifier for their access token, the handler never calls setOauthToken() to reassign the returned credentials to the TwitterOAuth client, causing the subsequent account/verify_credentials API call to remain signed with the site operator's stored Access Token and Access Token Secret rather than the authenticating visitor's token. This causes the X API to return the profile of the X application owner instead of the signing-in visitor, and the plugin then resolves and authenticates a WordPress account solely by matching that owner's email address via wp_set_auth_cookie(), allowing unauthenticated attackers to gain authenticated access as the WordPress user whose email corresponds to the X app owner, who is typically the site administrator.

items.title: jackson-databind validates the outer class of a class-name type ID but accepts attacker-selected classes inside its generic arguments, even when those classes violate the declar...
items.summary:
jackson-databind validates the outer class of a class-name type ID but accepts attacker-selected classes inside its generic arguments, even when those classes violate the declared type or would be rejected as direct type IDs. This bypasses the generic-argument validation added for CVE-2026-54512 (GHSA-j3rv-43j4-c7qm), of which this is an incomplete fix.



DatabindContext._resolveAndValidateGeneric() checks the outer class against the declared base type and then passes each argument from the type ID to _validateTypeParameter(), which validates the argument against the outer base type rather than enforcing its corresponding declared generic binding. It also invokes validators with arguments that have not passed the subtype check those validators expect. Under the default DefaultBaseTypeLimitingValidator this accepts an unrelated class inside a generic subtype even when the same class is rejected as a direct type ID. Where an allowIfBaseType(...) rule approves the outer type, Jackson substitutes LaissezFaireSubTypeValidator, so the configured validator no longer restricts the embedded arguments. The element type of a plain array type ID such as [Lpkg.Gadget; is likewise left unvalidated once the array's base type is approved.



Affected paths include annotation-based class-name polymorphism with a default Jackson 3.x JsonMapper, configured default typing in both Jackson 2.x and 3.x, and integrations that expose that default typing. The default-validator case requires no application-authored validator: with @JsonTypeInfo(use = Id.CLASS), a direct gadget type ID is rejected as "Not a subtype", while a type ID naming a generic wrapper around the same gadget is accepted and deserialized, including attacker-supplied bean properties. Where class-name default typing permits Map, a property declared as Map<String,String> accepts HashMap<FileSystemXmlApplicationContext,String>; map-key discovery then passes the attacker-controlled JSON property name to the selected class's one-string constructor. With Spring on the classpath and attacker-controlled XML the application can load, that constructor loads the XML and invokes ProcessBuilder.start() under the application account, giving arbitrary command execution.



This issue affects com.fasterxml.jackson.core:jackson-databind from 2.10.0 and tools.jackson.core:jackson-databind from 3.0.0. Releases before 2.10.0 are not affected, because PolymorphicTypeValidator was introduced in jackson-databind 2.10.0.

items.title: MLflow is an open source AI engineering platform for agents, large language models, and machine learning models. From 3.12.0rc0 until 3.17.0, third-party scorer deserialization ...
items.summary: MLflow is an open source AI engineering platform for agents, large language models, and machine learning models. From 3.12.0rc0 until 3.17.0, third-party scorer deserialization in mlflow/genai/scorers/base.py accepts request-selected descendants of THIRD_PARTY_SCORER_ALLOWED_MODULES rather than requiring an exact allowed module. A caller can use MLflow artifact endpoints to place a Python module beneath a writable allowed package and submit its module and class through /ajax-api/3.0/mlflow/scorer/invoke. Scorer.model_validate_json() imports the module and constructs the class before trace processing. Authentication-disabled deployments permit this code execution without credentials, while basic-auth deployments require a principal capable of creating an experiment and run and uploading artifacts. In either configuration, the allowed scorer package must be writable by the server process. This issue is fixed in version 3.17.0.

items.title: Tornado: Event loop blocking and excess memory use from chunked bodies with many small chunks
items.summary:
### Summary

When Tornado reads an HTTP/1.1 body that uses chunked transfer encoding, it processes all chunks that have already arrived without yielding to the event loop. A client can send a body made of millions of 1-byte chunks, which blocks the event loop (and therefore every other connection served by that process) for the entire time it takes to parse the body. A body near the default `max_body_size` of 100 MB can block the process for close to a minute, and the attacker can repeat or parallelize these requests.

Bodies made of tiny chunks also consumed far more memory than their size: a handler that does not use `@stream_request_body` stored each chunk as a separate object, using roughly 20 times as much memory as the bytes received.

### Impact

All Tornado HTTP servers are affected when they receive a request body for a handler that reads it, which includes any handler that does not reject the request before the body is read. No authentication is required. Lowering `max_body_size` reduces the maximum blocking time and memory use for each request but does not remove the issue.

`SimpleAsyncHTTPClient` is affected in the same way when it reads a response from a malicious server.

### Patches

Fixed in Tornado 6.6. Tornado now yields to the event loop periodically while reading any body, combines small chunks before passing them to `data_received`, and stores non-streaming bodies more compactly.

Applications using `@stream_request_body` should note that the pieces passed to `data_received` no longer correspond to HTTP chunk boundaries.

### Workarounds

- Run Tornado behind a reverse proxy that buffers request bodies and forwards them with a `Content-Length` header instead of chunked encoding.
- Lower `max_body_size` (for the whole server or for individual handlers) to limit the impact of each request.

### Credit

Reported by [uttej-badwane](https://github.com/uttej-badwane).

items.title: Tornado: Quadratic CPU usage when parsing HTTP headers with line folding
items.summary:
### Summary

Tornado's HTTP header parser takes quadratic time (O(n²)) when a header value is continued across many "obsolete line folding" (obs-fold) lines. An unauthenticated attacker can send a request whose header block is mostly short continuation lines. Parsing it uses a large amount of CPU on the IOLoop thread and blocks every other connection that process is serving.

This issue is closely related to CVE-2025-67725 (GHSA-c98p-7wgm-6p64). The fix for that advisory covered repeated headers but not line-folded continuations.

### Impact

All Tornado HTTP servers are affected. Header parsing runs before any application code, so no authentication or particular handler is required.

How bad it gets depends on `max_header_size`:

- **Default (64 KB):** each malicious request blocks the event loop for tens of milliseconds. Repeated requests can degrade service.
- **Raised `max_header_size`:** the cost grows with the square of the header size. A single 1 MB request can block the process for several seconds.

Only availability is affected. Confidentiality and integrity are not.

### Patches

Fixed in Tornado 6.6 by removing support for obsolete line folding completely; header lines that begin with whitespace are now rejected.

### Workarounds

- Keep `max_header_size` at its default value or lower it. This limits the impact but doesn't remove it.
- Run Tornado behind a reverse proxy that rejects or normalizes obsolete line folding before forwarding requests.

### Credit

Reported by @manus-pi.

items.title: When the `allowed_scopes` configuration is enabled, the OAuth2 token introspection mechanism does...
items.summary:
When the `allowed_scopes` configuration is enabled, the OAuth2 token introspection mechanism does not immediately invalidate a token in the cache after a revocation request. This results in a scenario where an access token that was introspected immediately before a revocation request may be returned again to the client after revocation, until the relevant cache entry is cleared.

The security consequence is that a revoked access token may be re-issued to the client during the cache lifetime. While the re-issued token is not treated as valid for API authorization, affected users may be unable to obtain a new valid access token until the cache is cleared, which can disrupt authentication flows.

items.summary: An access control bypass flaw was found in Samba's vfs_ceph_rgw module in it's openat() function. An authenticated user can bypass access controls to read or overwrite restricted files on shares configured with the experimental vfs_ceph_rgw module. When a client requests an existing file using mismatched character casing, the module fails to perform a case-insensitive lookup correctly, causing the server to treat the operation as creating a new file. As a result, the server skips standard permission checks on the existing file, allowing the attacker to access or overwrite sensitive data owned by other users.

Due to the improper implementation of access control rules, the WSO2 product accepts user-supplied input related to resource location without enforcing expected validation constraints. This can be exploited by an unauthenticated actor to direct the server to make requests to arbitrary network locations.

Exploiting this vulnerability allows a malicious actor to access both internal and external resources, available through the network or filesystem, that are reachable by the WSO2 product. This could potentially lead to unauthorized access to sensitive data and systems.

items.title: Electrum: Malicious server can replace a just-broadcast tx and try to trick user into RBF-ing it
items.summary:
### Summary

The main Electrum server the client connects to is trusted with mempool ("unconfirmed") transactions. This is documented [design](https://electrum.readthedocs.io/en/latest/faq.html#does-electrum-trust-servers). [0]

However now someone figured out a way to practically exploit it:
- when the client broadcasts a new tx1, a malicious server can swallow it,
- and update the client's history with a conflicting (invalid) tx2 that replaces the outputs with the attacker's output address.
- Tx2 has invalid signatures, but this is not checked (due to light client design).
- The wallet will display tx2 as an unconfirmed transaction - tx1 will not be displayed.
- If the client then manually RBF fee-bumps tx2, the client will sign it with a higher fee, and hence pay the attacker.

### Fixes

Commit 90fe30822 contains the fix [1], included in version 4.8.3.
The client now verifies the signatures of `wallet.is_mine` inputs for mempool txs (before adding them to its local history).

Users should upgrade (and regularly do so in any case).
As a workaround, without upgrading, when signing any transaction, for bumping the fee or not, they should verify the output addresses and amounts are as expected.

Clients that connect to servers they trust (e.g. run their own) are not affected.


### Remarks

- some servers are performing this attack in the wild
- electrum received two user-reports of this. user1 noticed after broadcasting tx1 the wallet history contained a different tx. user2 bumped the fee of tx2 and lost money.
- user1 reported tx1 was not propagated over the bitcoin p2p, so the server held it
- both reported the attacker's output address in tx2 was grinded to match the last four chars of the legit address from tx1
- based on user2's report, the server constructed a tx2 with zero fee (presumably in hope of the user bumping its fee)
- even with the fix, we still only validate "is_mine" inputs (i.e. paying from addresses that the wallet owns). So e.g. "incoming" txs are not validated. The client lacks a full consensus engine / script interpreter, though even with that, to cover non-is_mine inputs, it would have to validate the unconfirmed parents recursively until reaching mined txs. Mined txs we already SPV.


### Timeline

- 2026-10-11: user1 sends private disclosure, but the bump_fee vector is not realised
- 2026-10-18: user2 (Raju-K12) reports privately that they lost money after bump_fee
- 2026-10-23: version 4.8.3 git tagged, with the fix
- 2026-10-24: version 4.8.3 binaries released
- 2026-10-24: public disclosure


### Credits

Electrum thanks user1 and Raju-K12 for finding and responsibly disclosing this issue to us.

items.title: Seroval: Code injection through a typed array's own constructor property
items.summary:
### Summary

seroval writes a typed array as a call to its constructor. In affected versions, the constructor name in the output is read from a property that data on the value can replace, and it is written without checks. A typed array that received properties from untrusted data can then put arbitrary code into the serialized output.

### Details

Version 1.6.0 changed how seroval finds the class of an object, so that objects with their own `constructor` property serialize correctly. Typed arrays still took the constructor name from the value itself, so the name could come from the untrusted property instead of the array's real type.

These functions are affected:

- `serialize`, `serializeAsync`
- `crossSerialize`, `crossSerializeAsync`, `crossSerializeStream`
- the `Serializer` class
- `compileJSON`

`fromJSON` and `fromCrossJSON` are not affected: they only accept the names of the built-in typed arrays. With the `compactArrayBufferViews` option, the same lookup throws a `TypeError` instead of writing code.

### Impact

An application is affected only when it serializes a typed array that has an own `constructor` property set from untrusted data. That requires code that copies properties from untrusted objects onto a typed array. This is unusual, so the severity is rated Low, even though the result is script execution in the page that receives the output.

### Patches

Fixed in 1.6.11. The constructor name now comes from the array's internal type, which properties on the value cannot change. `compactArrayBufferViews` uses the real type as well.

### Workarounds

If you cannot upgrade, do not copy properties from untrusted objects onto typed arrays, or remove an own `constructor` property from a typed array before serializing it.

items.title: Seroval: Script injection through RegExp sources in serialized output
items.summary:
### Summary

seroval writes a `RegExp` as a regular expression literal. In affected versions, the `<` character in a `RegExp` source is written without escaping. A source built from untrusted input can then end the HTML `<script>` element that the serialized output is placed in, and run script in the page.

### Details

seroval escapes `<` in strings, so string values cannot end a `<script>` element. `RegExp` sources did not get the same escaping:

- Versions before 1.0.0 wrote the source as is.
- Version 1.5.5 stopped escaping `<` in `RegExp` sources, so that named groups and lookbehinds keep working. This removed the escaping for every `<` in a source.

These functions are affected:

- `serialize`, `serializeAsync`
- `crossSerialize`, `crossSerializeAsync`, `crossSerializeStream`
- the `Serializer` class
- `compileJSON`

`toJSON`, `fromJSON`, `toCrossJSON` and `fromCrossJSON` are not affected, because they never produce JavaScript.

### Impact

An application is affected when all of these are true:

1. It builds a `RegExp` from untrusted input that is used as regular expression syntax. Input passed through an escaping helper (such as an `escapeRegExp` function) is not enough to exploit this.
2. It serializes that `RegExp` with one of the functions above.
3. It places the output inside an HTML `<script>` element, as server rendering usually does.

In that case an attacker can run script in the page of any user who receives that output.

### Patches

Fixed in 1.6.10. A `RegExp` whose source contains `<` is now written with the `RegExp` constructor and an escaped string source. Named groups and lookbehinds keep working.

### Workarounds

If you cannot upgrade:

- Do not serialize a `RegExp` built from untrusted pattern syntax. Send its source and flags as strings, and build the `RegExp` on the client.
- Or reject patterns that contain `<` before they reach the serializer.

items.title: Seroval: fromJSON deserializer trusts node-supplied array length and sequence doneAt (unauthenticated event-loop DoS)
items.summary:
### Summary

`fromJSON` and `fromCrossJSON` used two node fields without checking them.

- An array node's element list was not checked to be an array. A small payload could set the length the decoder looped over. This part is also tracked in GHSA-wp97-x4hv-qvhp.
- A sequence node's done index was not checked. A crafted value produced an iterator that never finished.

### Impact

A service that passes untrusted input to `fromJSON` or `fromCrossJSON` can be made unavailable by an unauthenticated request.

- The array case blocks the thread while the decoder runs.
- The sequence case makes any code that reads the resulting iterator to the end run forever.

### Patches

Fixed in `seroval@1.6.8`.

- Element lists must be arrays.
- A sequence node's throw and done indices must be integers from -1 up to the last element index.

Invalid input throws `SerovalMalformedNodeError`.

### Workarounds

None. Upgrade to 1.6.8.

items.title: Seroval `fromJSON`/`fromCrossJSON` denial of service via unvalidated array node length
items.summary:
### Summary

`fromJSON` and `fromCrossJSON` did not check that an array node's element list is an array. A small crafted payload could set the length the decoder used. That length controlled how much memory was allocated and how many times the decoder looped, and it did not depend on the size of the payload.

### Impact

A service that passes untrusted input to `fromJSON` or `fromCrossJSON` can be made unavailable by an unauthenticated request.

- A small payload can allocate enough memory to end the process.
- A small payload can block the thread for seconds, or without end.

This affects any framework that decodes request bodies with these functions before its own validation runs.

This issue is a bypass of the fix for GHSA-66fc-rw6m-c2q6 in 1.4.1.

### Patches

Fixed in `seroval@1.6.8`. The deserializer now rejects any node whose element list is not an array, and throws `SerovalMalformedNodeError`.

### Workarounds

None. Upgrade to 1.6.8.

items.title: Seroval: Deserialization invokes attacker-chosen callables: AsyncIteratorFactoryInstance calls source.on(listener) without type check
items.summary:
### Summary

When `fromJSON` rebuilt an async iterator, it called `on()` on the iterator's source without checking that the source was a seroval stream. A crafted payload could pick another value as the source, such as a function returned by an application plugin. The deserializer then called that value's `on` method.

This is a variant of GHSA-mv8w-475r-vwqw. That fix covered the promise and stream control nodes but not the async iterator node.

### Impact

An application that passes untrusted input to `fromJSON` with plugins that return callable values can have those callables invoked during deserialization. What this allows depends on what the plugin's values do.

### Affected versions

- Versions up to 1.6.3 accept any value as the source.
- 1.6.4 rejects the reported payload.
- 1.6.5 to 1.6.7 check the source by node type, which a payload can get around by reusing a node id.
- All versions up to 1.6.7 should be treated as affected.

### Patches

Fixed in `seroval@1.6.8`. Streams and sequences are now internal class instances. The deserializer checks the source value with `instanceof`, so plain data and plugin values are rejected no matter which node id they use.

### Workarounds

Avoid plugins whose `deserialize` returns functions or objects with an `on` method when decoding untrusted input. Upgrading to 1.6.8 is recommended.

items.title: Mem0: Cross-tenant conversation leak via unescaped delimiter collision in session-scope key (_build_session_scope)
items.summary:
Summary

_build_session_scope() in mem0/memory/main.py builds the conversation-history scope key used to fetch/store the last N raw messages by naively joining caller-supplied user_id/agent_id/run_id values with unescaped & and = delimiters:

def _build_session_scope(filters):
    parts = []
    for key in sorted(["user_id", "agent_id", "run_id"]):
        val = filters.get(key)
        if val:
            parts.append(f"{key}={val}")
    return "&".join(parts)

_validate_and_trim_entity_id() (the only validation applied to these values) rejects only empty/whitespace-only strings — it never forbids & or =. This scope string is then used as an exact-match key against a SQLite column (storage.py: WHERE session_scope = ?) to fetch the last 10 raw messages for a given scope (main.py, Phase 0 of _add_to_vector_store, both sync and async).

Impact

Any caller who controls only their own run_id (or agent_id) — a very common integration shape, since apps frequently pass a client-/session-supplied identifier straight through as run_id without namespacing — can craft a value containing &user_id=<victim> (or &agent_id=<victim>) that produces a scope string byte-for-byte identical to a different tenant's real scope string.

Concretely: Tenant A calls add(msgs, user_id="alice", run_id="proj-x") → scope "run_id=proj-x&user_id=alice". An attacker who can only set run_id calls add(msgs, run_id="proj-x&user_id=alice") → identical scope string. The attacker's next add() call:

1. Reads Tenant A's raw prior conversation via get_last_messages(session_scope) and splices it verbatim into the attacker's own LLM fact-extraction prompt — a direct cross-tenant confidentiality leak (conversation content, potentially including PII, credentials, etc.).
2. Writes into the same colliding row-set via save_messages(), whose eviction logic (DELETE FROM messages WHERE session_scope = ? AND id NOT IN (...)) can evict/interleave Tenant A's history — permanent cross-tenant data corruption, not just a read.

Reachable via the public Memory.add() / AsyncMemory.add() API, and by extension the REST server's POST /memories endpoint (which takes run_id/agent_id straight from the request body).

Reproduction

from mem0.memory.main import _build_session_scope

# Tenant A: real user_id + run_id
scope_a = _build_session_scope({"user_id": "alice", "run_id": "proj-x"})
print(scope_a)  # "run_id=proj-x&user_id=alice"

# Attacker: controls only run_id, embeds a fake user_id inside it
scope_c = _build_session_scope({"run_id": "proj-x&user_id=alice"})
print(scope_c)  # "run_id=proj-x&user_id=alice"

assert scope_a == scope_c  # byte-for-byte collision

A full end-to-end proof (actual add() calls, no mocking of the vulnerable functions) confirms the attacker's subsequent add() call receives the victim's raw prior message content via get_last_messages.

Suggested Fix

Reject & and = in _validate_and_trim_entity_id(), alongside the existing whitespace check — this is the single validation chokepoint already used by every entry point (add, search, get_all, delete_all), so the fix is centralized. Alternatively/additionally, encode each component unambiguously (percent-encode each id, or use a length-prefixed/JSON-encoded scope key) so no valid-character combination in one field can ever collide with a different partition.

Also affected: TypeScript SDK (npm mem0ai)

The same flaw exists in mem0-ts/src/oss/src/memory/index.ts,
Memory.buildSessionScope(), which joins agent_id/run_id/user_id into the same
`key=value&key=value` string with the delimiters unescaped:

  private buildSessionScope(filters: SearchFilters): string {
    const parts: string[] = [];
    for (const key of ["agent_id", "run_id", "user_id"].sort()) {
      const val = (filters as any)[key];
      if (val) parts.push(`${key}=${val}`);
    }
    return parts.join("&");
  }

items.title: ONNX: Out-of-bounds read in ConvTranspose shape inference via undersized weight rank
items.summary:
## Summary

ONNX ConvTranspose shape inference performed an out-of-bounds read when the weight tensor had fewer than three dimensions and the model did not provide a `kernel_shape` attribute.

The inference function derived an empty `effective_kernel_shape` vector from the undersized weight tensor, then indexed that vector once for each spatial dimension of the input tensor. A crafted model passed `onnx.checker.check_model()` and caused SIGSEGV when passed to `onnx.shape_inference.infer_shapes()`.

## Technical details

For an input shape such as `[1, 1, 5]`, shape inference computes one spatial input dimension. A weight shape such as `[1, 3]` has no spatial dimensions, so deriving `kernel_shape` from dimensions 2 onward produces an empty vector. The output loop nevertheless accesses `effective_kernel_shape[0]`.

The defect affected both the older `convTransposeShapeInference_opset11()` path and the then-current ConvTranspose inference implementation.

## Impact

An application that performs shape inference on an untrusted model can be terminated, causing denial of service. The observed result was a deterministic process crash. No confidentiality or integrity impact was demonstrated.

## Affected versions

- Affected: ONNX 1.2.1 through 1.21.0
- Patched: ONNX 1.22.0

## Remediation

Upgrade to ONNX 1.22.0 or later. The fix rejects input and weight tensors with fewer than three dimensions before deriving the spatial kernel shape.

- Fix: [onnx/onnx#7997](https://github.com/onnx/onnx/pull/7997)
- Commit: [`2ec288908`](https://github.com/onnx/onnx/commit/2ec288908952eea9dcf48d4b197915e1f72c6abf)

The original malformed model was re-tested against the published ONNX 1.23.2 wheel and correctly raises `InferenceError`.

## Severity

The vulnerable ONNX component processes the malicious model through a local library API or file boundary and is not itself bound to a network stack. Applications that expose ONNX model processing over a network should calculate an Environmental score with Modified Attack Vector set to Network.

items.title: ONNX: Denial of service via unchecked expansion of packed sub-byte tensors in ONNX Python APIs
items.summary:
## Summary

ONNX's Python tensor-materialization helpers could allocate memory according to attacker-controlled tensor dimensions without verifying that a packed sub-byte payload contained the declared number of elements.

A very small model could therefore cause a disproportionately large allocation when an application called `onnx.numpy_helper.to_array()` or constructed `onnx.reference.ReferenceEvaluator` with the model. The issue affected `UINT2`, `INT2`, `UINT4`, `INT4`, and `FLOAT4E2M1` tensors stored in either `raw_data` or packed `int32_data`.

## Technical details

The vulnerable `_unpack_2bit()` and `_unpack_4bit()` paths first allocated a small array based on the available packed bytes, then resized it to the shape declared in `TensorProto.dims`. They did not first confirm that the payload encoded enough logical elements for that shape.

For example, the reporter demonstrated a 66-byte model containing one packed byte and a declared dimension of 700,000,000. The model passed `onnx.checker.check_model()` and allocated approximately 700 MB while materializing the initializer, followed by another large allocation when executing the reference evaluator.

Loading, checking, or running shape inference on the serialized model alone did not trigger the allocation. The vulnerable tensor had to be materialized.

## Impact

An application that materializes packed tensors from an untrusted model can exhaust available memory, causing denial of service. Memory corruption and code execution were not demonstrated.

## Affected versions

- Affected: ONNX through 1.21.0
- Patched: ONNX 1.22.0

## Remediation

Upgrade to ONNX 1.22.0 or later.

The primary fix validates the logical element count before resizing the unpacked NumPy array. A complementary checker change rejects an undersized packed payload before materialization.

- Materialization fix: [onnx/onnx#8033](https://github.com/onnx/onnx/pull/8033)
- Checker defense-in-depth: [onnx/onnx#8038](https://github.com/onnx/onnx/pull/8038)

The five affected tensor types and both storage formats were re-tested against the published ONNX 1.23.2 wheel and are rejected before the oversized allocation.

To verify the behavior using a released vulnerable package in an isolated environment, install `onnx==1.21.0` with `python -m pip install "onnx==1.21.0"`. Run memory-exhaustion demonstrations only with an appropriate process memory limit.

## Severity

The vulnerable ONNX component processes the malicious model through a local library API or file boundary and is not itself bound to a network stack. Applications that expose ONNX model processing over a network should calculate an Environmental score with Modified Attack Vector set to Network.

items.title: ONNX: Null Pointer Dereference in ScanInferenceFunction Due to Missing Required Attribute
items.summary:
## Summary

ONNX shape inference did not safely validate the required Scan `num_scan_inputs` attribute. Two malformed values could terminate or disrupt the process:

1. If the attribute was missing, `ctx.getAttribute("num_scan_inputs")` returned null and was dereferenced.
2. If the attribute was negative, conversion to `size_t` produced a very large value that reached a vector allocation and raised `std::length_error`.

The negative-value variant passed `onnx.checker.check_model()` before reaching shape inference.

## Technical details

The vulnerable Scan inference implementations used the following pattern:

```cpp
auto num_scan_inputs =
    narrow_cast<size_t>(ctx.getAttribute("num_scan_inputs")->i());
```

This code neither checked the returned pointer nor rejected a negative signed value before converting it to an unsigned size. The pattern was present in the current Scan inference function and the older opset 8 and 9 paths.

The fix uses the required-attribute helper and checked narrowing:

```cpp
auto num_scan_inputs =
    narrow<size_t>(getRequiredAttributeInt(ctx, "num_scan_inputs"));
```

## Impact

An application that performs shape inference on an untrusted model can be terminated or forced into an exceptional allocation path, causing denial of service. No confidentiality or integrity impact was demonstrated.

## Affected versions

- Affected: ONNX 1.4.0 through 1.21.0
- Patched: ONNX 1.22.0

ONNX 1.4.0 is the first release containing the vulnerable Scan shape-inference implementation.

## Remediation

Upgrade to ONNX 1.22.0 or later.

- Fix: [onnx/onnx#7916](https://github.com/onnx/onnx/pull/7916)
- Commit: [`dd6bc92ea`](https://github.com/onnx/onnx/commit/dd6bc92ea39fd2274fd671f0734b0b8b558356f5)

Both reported models were re-tested against the published ONNX 1.23.2 wheel and correctly raise `InferenceError`.

## Severity

The vulnerable ONNX component processes the malicious model through a local library API or file boundary and is not itself bound to a network stack. Applications that expose ONNX model processing over a network should calculate an Environmental score with Modified Attack Vector set to Network.

The two triggers remain in one advisory because they affect the same required attribute, share the same unsafe conversion path and remediation, and were fixed in the same release.

items.title: ONNX: Out-of-Bounds Read in RNN/GRU/LSTM Shape Inference (Old Opsets, Missing Rank Check)
items.summary:
## Summary

ONNX shape inference performed an out-of-bounds read when processing a malformed RNN, GRU, or LSTM node from opsets 1–6 whose first input had a rank other than three.

`RNNShapeInference_opset1_to_6()` checked whether the input shape was present but accessed `dim(0)` and `dim(1)` without first checking its rank. A crafted model could therefore terminate a process that called `onnx.shape_inference.infer_shapes()`. The model passed `onnx.checker.check_model()` before reaching the vulnerable path.

## Technical details

The vulnerable code read dimensions unconditionally:

```cpp
if (hasInputShape(ctx, 0)) {
  const auto& first_input_shape = getInputShape(ctx, 0);
  seq_length = first_input_shape.dim(0);
  batch_size = first_input_shape.dim(1);
}
```

For an undersized shape, protobuf's repeated-field access read outside the intended array in release builds. The observed result was SIGSEGV; sanitizer and debug builds terminated on a protobuf bounds check.

The newer opset 7–13 and opset 14+ inference paths already required the first input to have rank three and were not affected.

## Impact

An application that performs shape inference on an untrusted model can be terminated, causing denial of service. Exploitation does not require privileges or human interaction once the model is processed. No confidentiality or integrity impact was demonstrated.

## Affected versions

- Affected: ONNX through 1.21.0
- Patched: ONNX 1.22.0

The vulnerable schemas are limited to RNN and LSTM opsets 1–6 and GRU opsets 3–6.

## Remediation

Upgrade to ONNX 1.22.0 or later. The fix validates that the first input has rank three before accessing its dimensions.

- Fix: [onnx/onnx#7879](https://github.com/onnx/onnx/pull/7879)
- Commit: [`92e541266`](https://github.com/onnx/onnx/commit/92e541266af5dd38cfa48aeb92206f4268a066cd)

The original malformed model was also re-tested against the published ONNX 1.23.2 wheel and correctly raises `InferenceError`.

## Severity

The vulnerable ONNX component processes the malicious model through a local library API or file boundary and is not itself bound to a network stack. Applications that expose ONNX model processing over a network should calculate an Environmental score with Modified Attack Vector set to Network.

items.title: vLLM: Phi-4 multimodal audio encoder materializes and retains full attention matrices: a single max-length audio OOM-crashes the vLLM engine
items.summary:
### Summary

The Phi-4 multimodal audio encoder (`phi4mm_audio.py` / `phi4mm_utils.py`) runs its conformer attention in **eager mode by default**: the official HF config of `microsoft/Phi-4-multimodal-instruct` does not set `use_pt_scaled_dot_product_attention`, so the default `False` applies (`phi4mm_audio.py:166`, `:876`; `phi4mm_utils.py:1669`). The eager path fully materializes the attention probability matrix of shape `[n_chunks, 16, 500, 500]` per layer — and then **stores it on the module**: `self.attn = attn` (`phi4mm_utils.py:1802`, a `torch.jit.Attribute` declared at `:1693`), keeping a live reference for every one of the 24 encoder layers.

The only gates on audio length are the server-side limits `VLLM_MAX_AUDIO_CLIP_FILESIZE_MB=25` and `VLLM_MAX_AUDIO_DECODE_DURATION_S=600` (`envs.py:83-84`) — i.e. a 10-minute clip is a **legal input by default**. A 600 s clip becomes ~60,000 mel frames, which the encoder unfolds into 500-frame chunks (`phi4mm_audio.py:996`, `max_seq_len = 500`), giving `n_chunks ≈ 120`. Each layer therefore materializes a `120×16×500×500` matrix (~1–2 GiB depending on dtype), and the module attribute keeps all completed layers' matrices alive, so GPU memory climbs monotonically **within a single request** until an allocation fails.

Verified end-to-end on the official `vllm/vllm-openai:v0.31.0` image: one 19.2 MB silent 600 s WAV → worker `torch.OutOfMemoryError: CUDA out of memory. Tried to allocate 2.29 GiB ... 501.75 MiB free ... 22.09 GiB allocated by PyTorch` inside `get_audio_features` (`phi4mm_audio.py:1279` → `:1332` → `phi4mm_utils.py:1386`) → `EngineCore encountered a fatal error` → API `EngineDeadError` → whole server down; `/health` refuses connections. Total time from request to dead service: **~6 seconds**.

A secondary effect: because `self.attn` persists on the module after the request ends, the matrices of the last audio request stay resident indefinitely (observed +50 MiB pinned after a single 5 s control request); they are only overwritten by the next audio request, so the resident footprint equals the largest audio processed since startup.

### Details

**1. Root cause.** `MultiHeadedAttention.forward_attention` in eager mode computes `attn = masked_softmax(scores, mask)` and unconditionally executes `self.attn = attn` (`phi4mm_utils.py:1795-1802`). The attribute is a leftover inference/debug hook (used by `torch.jit.Attribute(None, Tensor | None)` at `:1693`); in serving it serves no purpose but pins the full `[batch·chunks, heads, T, T]` tensor per layer past both the layer's forward and the request's lifetime. The SDP attention branch (`use_pt_scaled_dot_product_attention=True`) never materializes this matrix — but the HF config does not enable it and the code default is `False`.

**2. Why one request suffices.** The conformer chunks long audio to `max_seq_len = 500` frames (`phi4mm_audio.py:996`). Duration is bounded only by `VLLM_MAX_AUDIO_DECODE_DURATION_S=600`, so `n_chunks` reaches ~120 for a maximal clip. With 16 heads and fp32 scores, one layer's attention tensor is ~1.8 GiB (the observed failing allocation was 2.29 GiB, consistent with the scores+bias materialization). The encoder has `num_blocks=24`, `attention_heads=16`, `attention_dim=1024`, `time_reduction=8` (HF config). Weights plus a handful of retained per-layer matrices exhaust the ~2.3 GiB headroom that `--gpu-memory-utilization 0.9` leaves on a 24 GB card — mid-forward, on the first request.

**4. Deployment reality.** `--trust-remote-code` is the documented, standard way to serve this model (the HF model card instructs it), so the finding applies to default deployments. The crash is deterministic, not load-dependent: scheduler stats at death show a single running request and near-zero KV cache usage.


### Impact

Any unauthenticated client that can reach the chat/completions API of a default deployment serving `Phi-4-multimodal-instruct` (or any model reusing this audio tower) can kill the entire engine

items.title: vLLM: Untrusted EPS inputs can trigger denial of service or Ghostscript RCE
items.summary:
### Summary

In vLLM 0.30.0, `ImageMediaIO` passes attacker-controlled image bytes to Pillow's format autodetection without restricting the accepted formats; the request's MIME label does not constrain decoder selection. An EPS payload labeled `image/png` reached the host's Ghostscript executable. On a host with Ghostscript affected by CVE-2024-29510, this exposes the known Ghostscript sandbox escape through vLLM's image-loading path and can execute commands with the vLLM process's privileges. A bounded marker-command payload executed through the PyPI wheel's actual `ImageMediaIO.load_base64()` implementation using Debian Ghostscript 10.03.0. The loader-level execution is reproduced; the HTTP request path is source-traced but was not exercised end to end. This report concerns vLLM's untrusted-format dispatch and does not claim a new Ghostscript vulnerability. Exploitation requires an image-capable request path, a caller able to reach it under the deployment's authentication policy, and a vulnerable host Ghostscript build.

### Details

`ImageMediaIO` is the boundary where attacker-controlled bytes enter Pillow's format autodetection: the declared MIME type does not constrain decoder selection, and the loader calls `Image.open(BytesIO(data))` without a Pillow format allowlist. Pillow recognizes EPS by its file signature, and vLLM's subsequent `image.load()` call enters Pillow's EPS processing path. The OpenAI chat multimodal parser reaches this path through [`parse_image()` and `fetch_image()`](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/blob/bc21cba9673cfc2256a2726b4bc32f062237cd35/vllm/entrypoints/chat_utils.py#L1077-L1081) and the [media connector](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/blob/bc21cba9673cfc2256a2726b4bc32f062237cd35/vllm/multimodal/media/connector.py#L367-L402); the data URL path extracts the MIME label and forwards the bytes to the loader ([source](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/blob/bc21cba9673cfc2256a2726b4bc32f062237cd35/vllm/multimodal/media/connector.py#L319-L332)). This is the vLLM-specific issue: untrusted image bytes can select a Pillow-supported format parser. Each downstream impact depends on the relevant parser, component version, and host configuration.

Pillow recognizes EPS by its file signature and invokes Ghostscript with `-dSAFER`, `-sDEVICE=pnmraw`, and the untrusted EPS input ([Pillow EPS plugin](https://github.com/python-pillow/Pillow/blob/12.3.0/src/PIL/EpsImagePlugin.py#L132-L159), [load path](https://github.com/python-pillow/Pillow/blob/12.3.0/src/PIL/EpsImagePlugin.py#L405-L415)). The command execution in this report uses the already-known Ghostscript CVE-2024-29510, which allows crafted PostScript to bypass `-dSAFER`; Ghostscript lists 10.03.1 as the upstream fixed version ([Ghostscript CVE details](https://www.ghostscript.com/releases/cve/index.html)). This is an N-day dependency chain: CVE-2024-29510 provides the command-execution primitive, while the vLLM-specific issue is that untrusted, remotely supplied image bytes can reach the affected interpreter. No new Ghostscript flaw is claimed here.

The vLLM Python requirements declare Pillow but not Ghostscript, so this execution chain depends on a Ghostscript executable supplied by the host or deployment image. I reproduced command execution with the PyPI `vllm==0.30.0` wheel, Pillow 12.3.0, and Debian amd64 Ghostscript `10.03.0~dfsg-1`. The Codean Labs CVE-2024-29510 testkit identified that Ghostscript build as vulnerable. The adapted EPS payload ran only `touch` on a temporary marker. The marker existed after the loader call, although Pillow then raised `ValueError` because the exploit changes Ghostscript's output device. The API route was traced in source but a model-backed HTTP request was not run. Only PyPI `vllm==0.30.0` was checked; no wider affected release range or other Ghostscript vendor build is claimed.

items.title: vLLM: Responses API bypasses trust_request_chat_template for chat_template_kwargs
items.summary:
## Summary

vLLM's `/v1/responses` endpoint accepts request-level `chat_template_kwargs`, but does not apply the `--trust-request-chat-template` gate that protects Chat Completions, render, tokenize, and pooling paths.

When the server is run with the documented default `trust_request_chat_template=False` and no explicit `--chat-template`, a Responses request can pass:

```json
{"chat_template_kwargs": {"chat_template": "<attacker Jinja template>"}}
```

That key is preserved by `ChatParams.get_apply_chat_template_kwargs()` and then bound as the `chat_template` parameter to the shared HF renderer. Prior vLLM advisories establish that request-controlled Jinja chat templates can cause CPU/memory exhaustion. This report covers the current-head Responses sibling path missed by the earlier fixes.

## Technical Details

The shared OpenAI frontend has a validation helper that rejects request-supplied chat templates unless the trust flag is enabled. It explicitly checks both top-level `chat_template` and `chat_template_kwargs["chat_template"]`.

Responses is a separate serving path:

- `vllm/entrypoints/openai/responses/protocol.py` exposes `chat_template_kwargs`.
- `ResponsesRequest.build_chat_params()` merges request kwargs.
- `OpenAIServingResponses._effective_chat_template_kwargs()` uses those kwargs.
- `ChatParams.get_apply_chat_template_kwargs()` preserves a request `chat_template` key when the server chat template is `None`.
- `vllm/renderers/hf.py` unpacks the result into `safe_apply_chat_template`.

There is no equivalent trust gate in `vllm/entrypoints/openai/responses/serving.py`.

## Impact

An authenticated caller who can submit `/v1/responses` requests can supply a request-controlled Jinja chat template despite the trust flag being disabled. The expected fixed behavior is the same as Chat Completions: reject `chat_template_kwargs["chat_template"]` unless the server was started with `--trust-request-chat-template`.

## Suggested Fix

- Add `trust_request_chat_template` to `OpenAIServingResponses`.
- Pass `args.trust_request_chat_template` when constructing the Responses serving object.
- Reject `request.chat_template_kwargs["chat_template"]` before rendering when trust is false.
- Keep ordinary kwargs such as `enable_thinking` working.
- Add regression tests for default-deny and opt-in-allow behavior on `/v1/responses`.

## Affected Package/Versions

Source sweep found the affected shape in:

- `v0.16.0`
- `v0.18.0`
- `v0.20.0`
- `v0.21.0`
- `v0.22.0`
- `v0.22.1`
- `v0.23.0`
- current checkout `470229c37efaf69c86e8bc97482b0b1ff7551c65`
- current `origin/main` `b3f0a0a0df76dda92ec4b2c9335f77e84adad911`

Suggested affected range:

```text
>= 0.16.0, <= 0.23.0
```

## Appendix: Duplicate Research

This is related to, but distinct from:

- `GHSA-6fvq-23cw-5628` / `CVE-2025-61620`
- `GHSA-69j4-grxj-j64p` / `CVE-2025-62426`

Those advisories establish the security impact of request-controlled Jinja templates and `chat_template_kwargs`, but they cover older Chat Completions/tokenize implementations. This report covers a current `/v1/responses` sibling path that still lacks the trust gate.

Local prior submissions this report..029 do not cover this root cause.

This advisory was fixed in [MR50300](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/50300).

items.title: The Envelope Layer: An Underestimated Surface of LLM Agent Defense
items.summary: Prior work framed the envelope layer as the channel through which malicious content enters an agent, and established it as a defense surface independent of the LLM layer and the agent layer; however, that work only tested the envelope layer briefly and did not examine how label strength, envelope authenticity, scaffold differences, or existing memories affect defense effectiveness. Following its GDA Measurement methodology and the A/B/C/D outcome taxonomy, this paper takes the A2A-TIBA attack as the test vehicle, uses the semantic breach rate as the primary indicator with the semantic refusal rate as its complementary reference, and characterizes the security boundary of the envelope layer through a two-by-two factorial experiment and a memory experiment. The results show that: when the envelope is authentic, strong labels consistently reduce the semantic breach rate, whereas weak labels are not necessarily better than an unlabeled baseline; when the envelope can be forged, the benefit of strong labels is weakened and its direction varies across frontends; and memory has a larger effect than any label manipulation: success memory raises the semantic breach rate while failure memory lowers it, and most combinations that contain both experiences return to the no-memory baseline. Accordingly, this paper refines the envelope layer from a single admission channel into two levels, an admission channel plus a context assembly surface, and argues that its security boundary is not a fixed property of labels but a dynamic outcome jointly shaped by label claims, frontend permissions, and historical memory.

items.title: Watermark Basins: Black-Box Detection of Distilled LLMs
items.summary: Proprietary language models and their reasoning traces are vulnerable to API-based distillation, where an adversary trains a student model on the teacher model's outputs. To obtain evidence of distillation, model providers can watermark the teacher's outputs, aiming to leave a radioactive signal in the student's outputs. Existing black-box detectors search for such radioactivity using token-level statistics of the suspect model's outputs. However, token-level signals are not always detectable, for instance when the distillation traces are sampled at a low temperature. In this work, we discover the watermark basin, a persistent signal that enables more reliable watermark detection: during fine-tuning, watermarked teacher traces embed a distinct, key-specific geometric signal in parameter space that lies orthogonal to the ordinary task-specific fine-tuning subspace. Building on this, we introduce Watermark Basin Alignment (WM-Basin), a black-box watermark detector that queries the suspect model through its API, without access to its weights or logits. WM-Basin maps generated text to gradient representations using a fixed clean probe model, projects out the ordinary fine-tuning task directions, and tests whether the residual gradient aligns with the watermark basin induced by the watermark key. We evaluate WM-Basin extensively across diverse teacher models and student architectures (from 135M to 8.2B parameters) distilled on mathematical reasoning. At a strict 0.1% false-positive rate, WM-Basin detects 79% of distilled models at n-gram=1 and 45% at n-gram=3, substantially improving over the state-of-the-art token-level baseline (29% and 1.3%, respectively). Because the watermark signal resides in a persistent basin, it survives post-distillation modifications including quantization, pruning, and reinforcement-learning post-training.

items.title: Blindfold: Keeping the Audit Coin Secret from LLM Agents
items.summary: Audit-based certification bounds the violation rate of an LLM agent by auditing a random fraction $\varepsilon$ of actions and reweighting the audited labels; its validity is meant to rest only on the defender's audit coin. We show that it also rests on a confidentiality property: the coin must not interfere with the agent's view before the action commits, at a time the agent chooses. We call this pre-commit noninterference (PNI) and measure its violation by $D_{\mathrm{A}}$, the total-variation distance between the agent's views under the two coin values. PNI is necessary and sufficient for an unbiased certificate against adaptive agents, the worst-case bias is $(1-\varepsilon)D_{\mathrm{A}}$, and no procedure that sees only audited labels can pay less. Leakage composes across steps, a resource shared across episodes opens a channel of computable size, and raising the audit rate cannot restore validity. On a monitor we built, a silent audit changes no output but adds latency that tool timestamps expose, and the agent can enlarge it. A real LLM agent follows an injection that names a visible audit notice (generic, tool, and timing clauses have no effect); over that channel the plain certificate fails on measured labels and, by a post-hoc analysis, in a live run on a pre-registered schedule, while a silent audit restores it. A fresh coin per audited call closes the timing channel; padding only narrows it.

items.title: PrivacyEvalClaw: A Tool-Augmented Deliberative Agent for Auditing Privacy Leakage in LLM Jailbreak Responses
items.summary: Reliable evaluation is a critical bottleneck in privacy red-teaming of large language models (LLMs): determining whether a jailbreak response actually reveals personal information can be difficult when disclosures are indirect, contextual, partial, or obfuscated. Existing evaluation approaches increasingly rely on guard models and LLM-as-Judges, yet these evaluators may interpret the same response differently. To better characterize this evaluation setting, we conduct a systematic study of privacy evaluators and find substantial disagreement, particularly in ambiguous cases that require additional evidence or targeted analysis to resolve. Motivated by these findings, we introduce \textsc{PrivacyEvalClaw}, a training-free deliberative agent for evaluating privacy leakage in LLM jailbreak responses. Rather than relying on isolated single-pass judgments, PrivacyEvalClaw treats evaluators and analysis modules as tools, adaptively gathers evidence, investigates uncertain disclosures, and reconciles conflicting signals before producing a final judgment. Our primary experiments use pairwise LLM-as-Judge evaluation of complete trajectories, showing that PrivacyEvalClaw achieves favorable win rates against competing baselines across outcome, process, and overall quality, while producing explicit reasoning traces that make the evaluation process more transparent and auditable.

items.title: What Victims Take Away: Attack Reuse and Defense Revision after Prompt-Injection Attacks
items.summary: Attack logs and red-team reports show targets the attacks used against them, to help them repair their defenses. Prompt injections against large language models (LLMs) are plain text, so such records also hand targets a working copy. Drawing on social learning theory and work on the victim-offender overlap, we study what targets do with that copy in Tensor Trust, an online game whose players defended LLM-guarded accounts, attacked one another's, and could read every attack they received. Using all 563,349 attack records, we compare each received attack with matched attacks that circulated among similar players at the same moment but never reached the target. Reuse mainly followed success: within a week, targets attacked other players with 10.0% of the attacks that had broken their defense, versus 0.03% of matched attacks (adjusted difference: 8.8-10.0 percentage points). Near-misses, whose replies began with "access granted" but that scored as failures, were reused about as rarely as failures: reuse tracked whether an attack paid off, not how its reply read, consistent with payoff-biased social learning. Breaches were also followed by defense changes, after which same-family attacks became 24.5 percentage points less successful against the target, relative to other defenders. Reuse came mainly from players already attacking, not newcomers. Previously received texts accounted for 23.2% of the successful hijacks we analyze. The attack history thus served both repair and reuse; we derive testable hypotheses for how AI security tools should disclose attacks, such as describing the technique without the full text.

items.title: Detecting and Mitigating Query-Based System Prompt Leakage Attacks
items.summary: Large Language Models (LLMs) rely on proprietary system prompts to enforce task directives, safety policies, and access controls. These prompts are vulnerable to query-based leakage attacks, where black-box adversaries extract confidential instructions through adaptive, multi-turn interactions. Existing defenses often assess queries independently, missing malicious behavior that emerges across interactions. We present AdvGuard, a model-agnostic framework for detecting and mitigating system prompt leakage. items.title: BUSTA: Teaching Small Language Models to Reason About Binary Execution

items.title: Bringing Hardware Security Education to All: A Seamless Curriculum Integration Approach
items.summary: Cybersecurity education has predominantly focused on software and network security, under the assumption that the underlying hardware is trustworthy. Threats introduced through the global semiconductor supply chain, together with vulnerabilities arising during design and integration, challenge the assumption that hardware can serve as an unquestioned root of trust. Sensor-enabled systems and machine-learning accelerators further expand the hardware attack surface. The undergraduate curriculum of electrical and computer engineering and computer science programs has not evolved accordingly. Core courses cover the design and the functionality of hardware while the security aspects remain overlooked, and dedicated hardware security (HS) courses are elective, scarce, and often restricted to graduate students. At the University of Florida, fewer than 7% of the undergraduate electrical and computer engineering students register for the introductory HS course each year. We present an integrated and economical approach that disseminates fundamental HS concepts within existing core courses through contextual learning. Nine hands-on modules were developed such that each security concept exercises an associated design concept of the core course, as a component of that course and not as a course of their own. Doing the security work is how the student exercises the design topic, so the modules are built to strengthen the host course and not only to add to it. Three were assessed across three offerings of the embedded systems course through one course survey and two conducted by an external evaluator, with 25 respondents. We report what those instruments measured and the limitations of the approach.

items.title: Log-To-Leak: Prompt Injection Attacks on Tool-Using LLM Agents via the Model Context Protocol
items.summary: LLM agents increasingly access external tools through the Model Context Protocol (MCP), but the natural-language metadata used to describe those tools creates a prompt-injection surface. Within this established tool-poisoning surface, we study Log-To-Leak, an additive post-hoc logging attack that induces a separate attacker-controlled call after the final legitimate call. Its payload targets the user query, MCP server name, server response, and agent response. We operationalize the injected directive through Trigger, Tool Binding, Justification, and Pressure, and separately measure call success, payload fidelity, and preservation of legitimate behavior. We evaluate five MCP servers and four LLM agents using five metrics spanning effectiveness, utility, and efficiency. Across 18 model-server pairs with valid tool execution, Log-To-Leak achieves an attack success rate (ASR) of 62.64-100% and conditional logging accuracy (LA) of 76.55-95.64%; 16 pairs have absolute target-task completion changes of at most 6.63 percentage points. Three evaluated defenses leave residual ASR above 55% on GitHub MCP with GPT-4o, while an instruction detector flags 85.53% of benign descriptions. These results show that successful task completion can coexist with unauthorized post-hoc disclosure and motivate host-controlled authorization for secondary tool calls.

items.title: Reva: Real-Time Vulnerability Detection through Contextual Probing of Large Language Models
items.summary: A vulnerability costs more to fix the later it is discovered. As coding agents generate code faster than developers can review it, software needs a first line of defense screening each new function in real time. LLM agents have recently become capable of finding real-world vulnerabilities by working as a security expert would: they run analysis tools, explore the surrounding code, test hypotheses and weigh the evidence before forming their own judgement. This reasoning, however, spans many model calls, so that each verdict takes minutes of compute, far too long for real-time screening. Faster detectors, which fine-tune deep learning models or prompt an LLM for a direct verdict, are less accurate: they judge a function without the context an agent gathers, and an LLM's generated verdict is unreliable even when given some of it. We present REVA (REal-time Vulnerability Analysis), an AI vulnerability detector that brings the security context and code understanding components behind agentic detectors into a single forward pass of an LLM. For each new function, REVA gives the LLM a pre-computed threat model of its module, lightweight static analysis findings and call-graph information. REVA leverages a trained probe to read the LLM's internal representations of the new function in this context. On PrimeVul's held-out test set, REVA on GLM-5.3-Flash reaches 60.0% accuracy in about one second per function. This matches VulTriage (59.2%), the state-of-the-art agentic detector, run on the same LLM, while being over 250 times faster and less than a tenth as costly. On the same prompt, the probe is 14% to 17% more accurate than the LLM's own direct verdict. Across three open LLMs, REVA is at least as accurate as VulTriage, and about 10% more accurate on two of them. An LLM's internal representations thus encode much of what agentic detectors obtain through reasoning.

items.title: Adversary Brains: Hypothesis-Based Logical Signatures for Threat Actor Detection with LLMs
items.summary: An adversary brain is an LLM-based model of a threat actor's behavior, held as an evolving logical signature: a hypothesis with enough structure that data can test it continuously, without a person re-interpreting it each time. Rather than any single observation, such as an IoC (Indicator of Compromise), it is the arrangement that becomes a detection, or intelligence, mechanism. Where YARA matches a file and Sigma matches a log line, an adversary brain matches the activity pattern of a campaign or threat actor. This is based on an intelligence analysis technique called Analysis of Competing Hypotheses (ACH), which the design lifts from the limitation of a few hypotheses at a time, to thousands, and then also operationalizes it for continuous detection purposes. Language models make the concept, and scale, practical: they turn prose reports into brains, judge matches, and drive the loop that keeps brains current. A partial pattern in a brain can also match a new value, such as a fresh C2 (command and control) domain name, assisting with the discovery of new indicators, and turning unknown unknowns into known unknowns, and potentially into knowns. The author would like to thank Ryan Moon for the collaboration, and Sounil Yu, Chris Inglis, Thomas Roccia, Marius Benthin, Israel Grimberg, Michal Kamensky, Justin Borland, Brandon Levene, John Hultquist, and John Bambenek for their feedback and assistance.

items.title: Then there is prompt injection, a malicious email, ...: The Wild Wide West of OpenClaw Agentic System Security
items.summary: AI-powered personal assistant frameworks such as OpenClaw combine LLM reasoning, persistent memory, tool invocation, local execution, and web-based workflows. These capabilities enable useful automation, but they also create security risks when untrusted inputs, model reasoning, tools, memory, and deployment configuration interact without explicit trust boundaries. This paper presents an empirical study of reported security concerns in OpenClaw using two complementary data sources: Reddit discussions and security-tagged GitHub issues. We analyze more than 25K Reddit posts from 13 OpenClaw-related subreddits and identify 162 security-relevant posts with 1,787 associated comments. We further collect 358 security-tagged GitHub issues and retain 180 issues describing concrete security concerns. Using qualitative analysis and evidence-grounded CWE mapping, we identify 521 CWE instances across 59 distinct weakness types, concentrated in access-control failures, sensitive-data exposure, injection, and unsafe execution. We also extract 543 practitioner mitigation suggestions and consolidate them into seven recurring strategies. To complement the empirical analysis, we present an evidence-grounded illustrative reconstruction of a representative sensitive-data exposure pathway using dummy secret values. Our findings show that OpenClaw security issues are not isolated implementation bugs; they reflect recurring trust-boundary failures across the agent execution pipeline. We discuss how these weaknesses map to both traditional software-security categories and agent-specific failure mechanisms, and derive implications for safer agentic systems, including explicit trust boundaries, least-privilege tool access, execution containment, runtime oversight, and defense-in-depth deployment.

items.title: Can Open Be Too Open? On the Security and Trustworthiness of Fully Transparent LLMs
items.summary: There are different levels of transparency for LLMs: open weights, open data, and/or open pipeline. Recently, more interest has emerged in fully transparent LLMs, i.e., LLMs with fully open weights, data, and training pipeline. Drawing analogies to other fields such as software security, it is often believed that increasing transparency inherently increases the security and trustworthiness of the LLM. However, we argue that such claims need to be critically re-evaluated in the context of LLMs. In this paper, we analyze the impact of transparency on LLM security and trustworthiness by reviewing the relevant literature. Our core findings are that, due to the limited reproducibility of LLM pipelines, in practice, users cannot verify the correspondence between open weights and the associated open data and pipeline. Thus, in order to trust a model, users still need to trust that developers acted honestly, reducing the benefits over models that provide less "transparency". Moreover, we find that even when LLMs are fully transparent and trusted, this openness can favor adversaries. Open weights in particular, but also open data and pipelines, can increase the success rate of attacks. Although the same mechanisms can be used to improve the model and protect it against attacks, the current lack of robust lightweight mechanisms to patch LLM vulnerabilities limits the benefits of openness at this time. We note that our analysis is based on current LLM capabilities and analysis tools, and that future developments may require a re-evaluation of these points.

items.title: GuardRAG: A Post-Retrieval Defense against Poisoning Attacks in Retrieval-Augmented Generation
items.summary: Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) enhances the factual grounding of Large Language Models (LLMs) by incorporating external evidence, but also exposes them to corpus poisoning attacks. In particular, coordinated attacks can introduce multiple mutually reinforcing poisoned documents into retrieved contexts, making reliable evidence filtering challenging. To address this problem, we propose GuardRAG, a training-free and plug-and-play post-retrieval defense that exploits the semantic structure of retrieved evidence to identify suspicious document groups. Specifically, GuardRAG first expands the retrieval range and removes near-duplicate candidates, then partitions the retained documents using Hierarchical Agglomerative Clustering (HAC) with a query-adaptive threshold. Finally, it scores and prunes suspicious clusters based on query relevance, cluster size, and semantic compactness. Experiments across three question-answering datasets, multiple poisoning attacks, and six LLMs demonstrate that GuardRAG substantially reduces attack success rates while maintaining answer utility under clean retrieval.

items.title: Steering for Safety, Hijacking for Profit: Trojan Threats in the LLM Activation Steering Supply Chain
items.summary: As large language models (LLMs) are increasingly integrated into Web search, online recommendation, and intelligent decision-making, the third-party plugin ecosystem centered on model customization continues to grow. Among these, Steering Vectors guide model behavior by intervening in internal representations. However, the open plugin ecosystem also introduces new supply-chain security risks: malicious plugins can disguise themselves as having legitimate functionality and covertly manipulate outputs without significantly affecting model performance. Although this risk poses a real threat, the security issues of Steering plugins in the LLM supply-chain ecosystem still lack systematic research. This paper audits eight mainstream open-source Steering plugin libraries and reveals three structural vulnerabilities: insufficient distribution integrity verification, excessive plugin privileges, and missing runtime monitoring, which offers an attack surface for attackers. To investigate this threat, we propose a malicious plugin, IDH. Specifically, IDH designs a norm-gated mutually exclusive routing mechanism and proposes an information-decay inflection point localization method to automatically select the injection layer, thereby simultaneously achieving benign and malicious functions. To counter such threats, we propose a runtime defense framework, by suppressing anomalous activation interventions and orthogonalizing inter-layer trajectory. We evaluate IDH across five mainstream LLMs, using safety-refusal steering as the legitimate functionality and commercial recommendation manipulation as the hijack objective. Experiments covering six brands across three commercial domains demonstrate that IDH achieves an attack success rate (ASR) of up to 97.8% while preserving high refusal rates on harmful requests.

items.title: The Target Agent Is Its Own Best Critic but a Poor Proposer: Self-Improved Red Teaming
items.summary: Automatic red teaming increasingly relies on large language models (LLMs) to iteratively diagnose failed attacks and propose improved adversarial prompts or injections. Although prior work strengthens this loop through prompt engineering and search-harness design, the mechanisms underlying its two core roles, criticism and attack proposal, has not been explored. To further investigate the core roles and therefore improve red teaming effectiveness, we disentangle two design choices: whether criticism is generated by the target session itself (self-criticism) or by a separately instantiated critic (external criticism), and whether that criticism is translated into the next attack by the target session (self-proposal) or by a separate attacker (external proposal). Through our analysis, we find that self-criticism is more effective because it is grounded in the target's live execution context, including observations, constraints, and available reasoning; removing reasoning reduces downstream attack success by 6%-17%. In contrast, self-proposal is substantially less effective because awareness of the adversarial objective induces explicit refusal and non-refusal sandbagging. These findings motivate a role-separated red-teaming approach: the target session diagnoses why an attack failed, while a separately instantiated attacker generates the next proposal. On DTAP-BENCH, spanning Telecom, Workflow, CRM, and Code domains, under both direct misuse and indirect threat models, as well as multiple agent frameworks, this configuration achieves 63.2% overall attack success rate (ASR), much higher than baselines. Our results show that effective automatic red teaming depends not only on model capability and search strategy, but also on how execution context and adversarial responsibility are distributed across model sessions.

items.title: Scope-Gap Injection: Exploiting Evaluator Channel Blind Spots in the OpenClaw Agent Security Competition
items.summary: This paper introduces Scope-Gap Injection (SGI), an indirect prompt injection method for multi-stage LLM-agent safety pipelines. Our observations suggest a scope gap: S2 appears to inspect the task instruction and skill definition without inspecting attachment contents, while the agent reads attachments during S3. SGI keeps the visible task and skill benign, while target identifiers, bypass parameters, and authorization procedures are moved into an attachment written as a business worklist. The S2 judge therefore sees a harmless task, while the agent follows the hidden worklist and triggers the permission bypass. In OpenClaw, SGI bypassed all three stages for 5 of 19 targets. The highest-scoring single submission achieved $F = 0.385$. Across the submission campaign, attachment placement was associated with higher aggregate S2 acceptance than in-skill placement: 78% versus 23%. We close with defenses that align evaluator scope with the channels available to the agent.
